macro.signature: array(val1, val2, ...) | array(key1 => val1, key2 => val2, ...)
macro.description: Creates an array from a list of values. The fundamental array constructor in IMathAS — used wherever an array literal is needed. Supports both numeric-indexed (sequential) and associative (key => value) forms. Values may be scalars, strings, or nested array() calls.
macro.example: 1) array(1,2,3) creates a numeric array with indices 0,1,2. 2) array("a"=>"x","b"=>"y") creates an associative array. 3) array(array(1,2),array(3,4)) creates a 2×2 nested array (matrix). 4) array(10,20,30)[1] returns 20.
macro.gotcha: Indices start at 0 — array(1,2,3)[0] is 1, not array(1,2,3)[1]. Mixing integer and string keys is allowed but iteration order may be surprising. Nested array() calls are the standard way to build matrices — all inner arrays must share the same length for matrix operations to work correctly. An empty array() is valid; count(array()) returns 0.

macro.description: Removes duplicate values from array and returns the result. Alias for PHP array_unique. The first occurrence of each value is kept.
macro.example: 1) array_unique(array(1,2,2,3,3,3)) returns array(0=>1,1=>2,3=>3). 2) array_unique(array("a","b","a")) returns array(0=>"a",1=>"b").
macro.gotcha: Keys are preserved (not reindexed) — use values of the result if you need a clean 0-indexed array. Comparison is done as strings, so 1 and "1" are treated as equal.

macro.description: Applies a math expression (todo) to each element of array and returns the resulting array. The placeholder variable in todo is x, which maps to each element in turn.
macro.example: 1) calconarray(array(1,2,3), "x^2") returns array(1,4,9). 2) calconarray(array(0,1,2), "2*x+1") returns array(1,3,5).
macro.gotcha: todo is parsed by mathphp and evaluated per element — only expressions allowed by mathphp are valid. Does not support multi-variable expressions; use multicalconarray for that. Returns false if evaluation fails.

macro.description: Like calconarray but applies todo only to elements where the condition ifcond evaluates true. Elements that fail the condition are returned unchanged.
macro.example: 1) calconarrayif(array(1,2,3,4), "x*10", "x>2") returns array(1,2,30,40). 2) calconarrayif(array(-1,0,1), "x^2", "x<0") returns array(1,0,1).
macro.gotcha: Both todo and ifcond are parsed by mathphp; the element placeholder is x in both expressions. Condition and transform are applied per-element in a single pass — there is no way to reference neighboring elements. Returns false on evaluation error.

macro.description: Generates an array of evenly spaced numbers from min to max inclusive, stepping by step (default 1). Both endpoints are included when the range aligns to the step.
macro.example: 1) consecutive(1, 5) returns array(1,2,3,4,5). 2) consecutive(0, 1, 0.25) returns array(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1). 3) consecutive(10, 1, -1) produces a downward sequence.
macro.gotcha: If step is 0, the internal for-loop runs forever — always ensure step is nonzero. Float step values may produce rounding artifacts at the endpoints. Use sortarray to reorder afterward if needed.

macro.description: Returns the number of elements in array. Alias for PHP count.
macro.example: 1) count(array(1,2,3)) returns 3. 2) count(array()) returns 0.
macro.gotcha: Passing a non-array scalar returns 1 in PHP (not 0), which can be misleading. Use is_array first to guard against accidentally counting a scalar. Does not count recursively — nested arrays count as one element each.

macro.description: Returns values in a1 that are not present in a2. Wrapper for PHP array_diff. The operation is asymmetric — order of arguments matters.
macro.example: 1) diffarrays(array(1,2,3,4), array(2,4)) returns array(0=>1, 2=>3). 2) diffarrays(array("a","b","c"), array("b")) returns array("a","c").
macro.gotcha: Only values from a1 are returned — values in a2 that are absent from a1 are ignored. Keys from a1 are preserved, not reindexed. Comparison is string-based. Pair with intersectarrays and unionarrays for full set-algebra operations.

macro.description: Creates an array filled with value. If n_or_keys is an integer, returns an array of n elements starting at startIndex (default 0). If n_or_keys is an array, returns an associative array with those keys all set to value.
macro.example: 1) fillarray(0, 3) returns array(0,0,0). 2) fillarray(0, 3, 1) returns array(1=>0, 2=>0, 3=>0). 3) fillarray("x", array("a","b")) returns array("a"=>"x","b"=>"x").
macro.gotcha: When n_or_keys is an array of keys, startIndex is ignored. Numeric keys in key-mode are not reindexed — they remain as provided. Use consecutive + fillarray together to build indexed numeric ranges.

macro.description: Returns an array of values that appear in both a1 and a2. Wrapper for PHP array_intersect. Keys from a1 are preserved for matching values.
macro.example: 1) intersectarrays(array(1,2,3,4), array(2,4,6)) returns array(1=>2, 3=>4) (preserves a1 keys). 2) intersectarrays(array("a","b","c"), array("b","c","d")) returns array(1=>"b", 2=>"c").
macro.gotcha: Keys from a1 are preserved, not reindexed — use array_values in PHP if you need a clean 0-indexed result. Comparison is string-based. Only two arguments are accepted; for multi-array intersection chain calls.

macro.description: Returns true if value is an array, false otherwise. Alias for PHP is_array. Use this to guard functions that require array input.
macro.example: 1) is_array(array(1,2,3)) returns true. 2) is_array("hello") returns false. 3) is_array(0) returns false.
macro.gotcha: Returns false for all non-array types including strings, numbers, and null. Commonly used before calling count, sortarray, or other array functions to avoid unexpected behavior on scalar input.

macro.description: Joins array elements into a single string using separator (default ","). If ksort is true, the array is sorted by key before joining.
macro.example: 1) joinarray(array("a","b","c")) returns "a,b,c". 2) joinarray(array("a","b","c"), " | ") returns "a | b | c". 3) joinarray(array(2=>"z", 1=>"a"), ",", true) returns "a,z" (key-sorted).
macro.gotcha: Unlike arraytolist, joinarray supports any separator string. ksort reorders elements by key before joining, which matters for associative arrays. Non-scalar elements are coerced to string.

macro.description: Sorts multiple arrays together by the values of the first array in ascending order, applying the same permutation to all other arrays. Returns an array of arrays in the new order.
macro.example: 1) jointsort(array(3,1,2), array("c","a","b")) returns array(array(1,2,3), array("a","b","c")).
macro.gotcha: Requires at least two array arguments — fewer or non-array inputs produce an error echo and return []. All additional arrays must have the same length as the first; a mismatch returns the original inputs without the first array. The first array is reindexed 0..n-1 in the output.

macro.description: Filters array and returns only the elements for which condition evaluates true. The element is available as x in the condition expression.
macro.example: 1) keepif(array(1,2,3,4,5), "x>3") returns array(4,5). 2) keepif(array(-2,-1,0,1,2), "x>=0") returns array(0,1,2).
macro.gotcha: Condition is parsed by mathphp — only mathphp-supported comparison expressions are valid. The returned array is re-indexed from 0. Returns false on evaluation failure. For element-wise transformation use calconarrayif; keepif only filters, it does not transform.

macro.description: Merges two or more arrays left-to-right using PHP array_merge semantics. Numeric keys are reindexed; string keys from later arrays overwrite earlier ones.
macro.example: 1) mergearrays(array(1,2), array(3,4)) returns array(1,2,3,4). 2) mergearrays(array("a"=>1), array("a"=>2,"b"=>3)) returns array("a"=>2,"b"=>3).
macro.gotcha: Numeric keys are always reindexed from 0 in the merged result — original numeric keys are lost. String keys from later arrays silently overwrite earlier values. Use unionarrays if you want unique values rather than key-based merging.

macro.description: Evaluates a multi-variable math expression (todo) element-wise across multiple input arrays. vars is a comma-separated list of variable names that map positionally to the input arrays.
macro.example: 1) multicalconarray("a+b", "a,b", array(1,2,3), array(10,20,30)) returns array(11,22,33). 2) multicalconarray("a*b-c","a,b,c", arr1, arr2, arr3) applies the formula element-wise.
macro.gotcha: All input arrays must be the same length, and the number of variable names in vars must match the number of array arguments — mismatches return false with an error echo. Variable names are sanitized to word characters only. todo uses (varname) syntax which is internally rewritten to ($varname).

macro.description: Sorts an array by value or by key depending on dir. Accepts dir values: "asc" (default, ascending), "rev" (descending), "key" (sort by key), "keyfill" (fill missing numeric keys then sort by key). If input is a string, it is first parsed with listtoarray.
macro.example: 1) sortarray(array(3,1,2)) returns array(1,2,3). 2) sortarray(array(3,1,2),"rev") returns array(3,2,1). 3) sortarray(array(3,1,2),"key") sorts by keys.
macro.gotcha: dir="keyfill" requires maxkey to define the upper bound for gap-filling; missing keys are set to empty string before sorting. Numeric comparison is used for values where possible. String input is parsed by listtoarray first, so comma-separated lists work.

macro.description: Returns a copy of array with a splice applied: removes length elements starting at offset and optionally inserts replacement elements. Uses PHP array_splice semantics and reindexes the result.
macro.example: 1) splicearray(array(1,2,3,4,5), 1, 2) returns array(1,4,5) (removes 2 elements at index 1). 2) splicearray(array(1,2,3), 1, 0, array(10,20)) returns array(1,10,20,2,3) (inserts without removing).
macro.gotcha: Operates on a copy — the original array is not modified. Negative offset counts from the end like PHP array_splice. Replacement defaults to [] (empty). If length is omitted, all elements from offset to end are removed.

macro.description: Extracts selected elements from array by individual indices and/or inclusive ranges specified as "i:j". Can also pass a single array as the second argument to supply the list of selectors. Missing single indices yield an empty string.
macro.example: 1) subarray(array("a","b","c","d"), 0, 2) returns array("a","c"). 2) subarray(array(10,20,30,40,50), "1:3") returns array(20,30,40). 3) subarray(array(1,2,3,4,5), array(0,"2:4")) returns array(1,3,4,5).
macro.gotcha: Range endpoints run through evalbasic, so simple expressions like "n:n+2" work. If a range endpoint is non-numeric after evaluation, the range is skipped with an error echo. Ranges are inclusive on both ends using array_slice.

macro.description: Returns an array containing all unique values from both a1 and a2. Implemented as array_unique(array_merge(a1, a2)).
macro.example: 1) unionarrays(array(1,2,3), array(2,3,4)) returns array(1,2,3,4). 2) unionarrays(array("a","b"), array("b","c")) returns array("a","b","c").
macro.gotcha: Uniqueness is based on string comparison of values. Order of elements follows merge order with duplicates removed by first-occurrence rule. Only accepts exactly two array arguments — for more, chain calls or use mergearrays + array_unique manually.

macro.description: Computes the difference quotient (f(a+h) - f(a)) / h for a given function expression string, variable name, point a, and step size h. Returns a numeric value. Intended for numerical calculation, not symbolic differentiation.
macro.example: 1) calculusdiffquotient("x^2", "x", 3, 0.001) — returns approximately 6.001 (numerical approximation of derivative of x^2 at x=3). 2) calculusdiffquotient("sin(x)", "x", 0, 0.0001) — returns approximately 1.0 (derivative of sin at 0).
macro.gotcha: Passing h=0 causes division by zero — there is no guard against it. If the function string is invalid or cannot be parsed by makeMathFunction(), the macro returns 0 silently. Results are numerical approximations only; they are not exact derivatives. Do not use this to produce symbolic answers — use it only when a numerical difference quotient value is specifically required by the problem.

macro.signature: calculusnumint(func, var, a, b, n, method)
macro.description: Approximates the definite integral of func over [a, b] using n subdivisions and the specified numerical method. Supported methods are: left, right, midpoint, trapezoidal, simpsons. Returns a numeric approximation.
macro.example: 1) calculusnumint("x^2", "x", 0, 1, 100, "simpsons") — returns approximately 0.3333 (Simpson's rule with 100 subdivisions). 2) calculusnumint("x^2", "x", 0, 1, 4, "left") — returns 0.21875 (left Riemann sum, 4 subdivisions). 3) calculusnumint("sin(x)", "x", 0, 3.14159, 1000, "trapezoidal") — approximates integral of sin over [0, pi].
macro.gotcha: Simpson's method requires n to be even — passing an odd n causes an error and returns false. Passing n <= 0 also returns false with an error message. If a == b the result is 0. An invalid or unparseable func string causes the macro to return 0. The trapezoidal and Simpson's methods use n+1 evaluation points, while left/right/midpoint use n points. This library is for numerical work only — not a substitute for symbolic integration.

macro.description: Returns the sum of two or more complex numbers in standard form as a paired value [Re, Im]. Pass all addends as paired values inside a single array. Use roundto to control decimal precision.
macro.example: 1) $z = cx_add(array([2,-3],[0,-5])) gives [2, -8] (sum of 2-3i and -5i). 2) $z = cx_add(array([2,-3],[0,-5],[sqrt(2),-1])) gives [2+sqrt(2), -9] (three addends). 3) $z = cx_add(array([1,1],[-1,-1])) gives [0, 0].
macro.gotcha: All complex numbers must be in standard form [Re, Im]; polar form input is not supported. The result is always in standard form regardless of input arrangement.

macro.description: Returns the argument (angle theta) of a complex number as a float. Input num is [Re, Im] in standard form. argin controls whether the result is in radians (default) or degrees.
macro.example: 1) $theta = cx_arg([1,1]) gives pi/4 (approx 0.785398...) in radians. 2) $theta = cx_arg([1,1], "deg") gives 45 (degrees). 3) $theta = cx_arg([-1,0]) gives pi (approx 3.14159...).
macro.gotcha: Default argin is "rad"; set argin="deg" explicitly for degree output. Returns a scalar float, not an array. The argument is in the range (-pi, pi] (atan2 convention).

macro.description: Returns the complex conjugate of a complex number. The conjugate of (a+bi) is (a-bi), so the imaginary part is negated. Returns the result as a paired array [Re, Im].
macro.example: 1) $w = cx_conj([3, -4]) gives [3, 4] (conjugate of 3-4i). 2) $w = cx_conj([0, 5]) gives [0, -5] (conjugate of 5i). 3) $w = cx_conj([-2, 0]) gives [-2, 0] (real number unchanged).
macro.gotcha: Input must be in standard form [Re, Im]. The real part is unchanged; only the sign of the imaginary part is flipped. Output format mirrors input format.

macro.description: Returns the three roots of a cubic equation f(x) = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d. coeff is the coefficient array [a, b, c, d]. Real roots are returned as [r] and complex roots as [Re, Im].
macro.example: 1) $roots = cx_cubicRoot([1,0,0,-1]) gives array([1],[...],[...]) — roots of x^3 - 1 = 0. 2) $roots = cx_cubicRoot([1,-6,11,-6]) gives array([1],[2],[3]) — three real roots. 3) $disp = cx_cubicRoot([1,0,0,-1], True) gives display strings for $showanswer.
macro.gotcha: When disp=True the function returns formatted strings for display only — do not use in calculations. Output root format depends on whether roots are real ([r]) or complex ([Re, Im]); check the type before indexing.

macro.description: Returns the quotient of two complex numbers in standard form as [Re, Im]. Pass exactly two complex numbers as paired values: [dividend, divisor]. The result is dividend / divisor.
macro.gotcha: Exactly two complex numbers must be provided: first is dividend, second is divisor. Division by zero (both Re and Im of divisor are 0) will cause an error. Result is always in standard form.

macro.description: Returns a display string of one or more complex numbers in polar form: r (cos(t) + i sin(t)). Accepts standard form input [Re, Im] and converts to polar for display. Suitable for $showanswer.
macro.example: 1) $s = cx_format2pol([1,1]) gives a string like "1.414 (cos(0.785) + i sin(0.785))". 2) $s = cx_format2pol([1,1], "deg") gives "1.414 (cos(45) + i sin(45))". 3) $s = cx_format2pol(array([1,1],[0,2])) gives an array of two polar-form strings.
macro.gotcha: Note: despite the parameter name argin, the default is "rad" for radian output. The note in the source says default is "deg" but actual default in code is "rad" — verify with your version. Returns a string, not a numeric array; do not use in arithmetic.

macro.description: Returns a display string of one or more complex numbers in standard form: a + b i. Accepts standard form input [Re, Im]. Suitable for $showanswer or displaying intermediate results.
macro.example: 1) $s = cx_format2std([3,-4]) gives "3-4 i". 2) $s = cx_format2std([0,2]) gives "2 i". 3) $s = cx_format2std(array([1,1],[-2,3])) gives array("1+1 i", "-2+3 i").
macro.gotcha: Returns a formatted string, not a numeric array — do not use the output in further calculations. Default rounding is 3 decimal places, which differs from the 12-place default used by arithmetic functions.

macro.description: Returns the row echelon form (REF) or reduced row echelon form (RREF) of a matrix A that may contain real or complex entries. Each row is an array; complex entries are given as [Re, Im], real entries as a single number.
macro.example: 1) $M = cx_matrixreduce(array([1,[2,3]],[[0,-1],5])) returns REF of a 2x2 complex matrix. 2) $M = cx_matrixreduce(A, True) returns RREF. 3) $Mdisp = cx_matrixreduce(A, False, True) returns formatted string matrix for display.
macro.gotcha: When disp=True, the output is a formatted string matrix for display only — do not use in arithmetic. Real entries are plain scalars; complex entries must be entered as paired arrays [Re, Im] within rows. rref defaults to False (REF).

macro.description: Returns the modulus (absolute value) of a complex number as a float, computed as sqrt(Re^2 + Im^2). Input num is [Re, Im] in standard form.
macro.example: 1) $r = cx_modul([3,4]) gives 5. 2) $r = cx_modul([1,1]) gives sqrt(2) (approx 1.41421356...). 3) $r = cx_modul([-2,0]) gives 2.
macro.gotcha: Returns a scalar float, not an array. Input must be a single complex number in standard form [Re, Im]. Use cx_std2pol to get both modulus and argument together as [mod, arg].

macro.description: Returns the product of two or more complex numbers in standard form as a paired value [Re, Im]. Pass all factors as paired values inside a single array. Supports multiplying more than two numbers at once.
macro.example: 1) $z = cx_mul(array([2,-3],[1,1])) gives [5,-1] — (2-3i)(1+i). 2) $z = cx_mul(array([0,1],[0,1])) gives [-1,0] — i*i = -1. 3) $z = cx_mul(array([2,0],[3,0],[4,0])) gives [24,0] — product of three real numbers.
macro.gotcha: All inputs must be in standard form [Re, Im]. Unlike cx_div, you can pass more than two numbers. Result is always in standard form; use cx_std2pol to convert if polar output is needed.

macro.description: Returns a graphical plot of a complex number on the complex plane, showing the point, vector, and optionally labels for Re, Im, modulus, argument, and z. Input is a single complex number [Re, Im].
macro.example: 1) $img = cx_plot([3,4]) plots z = 3+4i with degree labels shown. 2) $img = cx_plot([1,1], "rad") plots z = 1+i with radian angle labels. 3) $img = cx_plot([2,-3], "deg", 2, False) plots without any labels.
macro.gotcha: argin defaults to "deg" (degrees) for plot labeling — this differs from most other cx_ functions that default to "rad". Only a single complex number can be plotted per call. Output is a display image string, not a numeric value.

macro.description: Converts a complex number from polar form [mod, arg] to standard form [Re, Im]. Input num is [modulus, argument]; argin specifies whether the argument is in radians or degrees.
macro.example: 1) $z = cx_pol2std([2, pi/4]) gives [sqrt(2), sqrt(2)] — r=2, theta=45deg in radians. 2) $z = cx_pol2std([1, 90], "deg") gives [0, 1] — unit complex at 90 degrees. 3) $z = cx_pol2std([5, 0]) gives [5, 0] — real number.
macro.gotcha: Input num must be in polar form [mod, arg], not standard form [Re, Im] — this is the reverse of cx_std2pol. Default argin is "rad"; if your argument is in degrees pass argin="deg" explicitly.

macro.description: Returns the Euler polar form of one or more complex numbers as a display string: z = re^(itheta). Input is in standard form [Re, Im]. Suitable for $showanswer with Euler notation.
macro.gotcha: Returns a string for display only — not suitable for arithmetic. Default argin is "rad". When multiple complex numbers are passed the return is an array of strings.

macro.description: Returns the power of a complex number raised to exp, in standard form as [Re, Im]. Uses De Moivre's theorem internally via polar conversion. exp can be any real number including fractions.
macro.gotcha: Returns a single result in standard form [Re, Im]; for all nth roots use cx_root instead. Fractional exponents return the principal root only. Input num must be in standard form.

macro.description: Returns an array of formatted string roots of the quadratic equation f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c. Real roots come as array("r1","r2") smallest to largest; complex roots as array("a+bi","a-bi"). Designed for use with $showanswer.
macro.example: 1) $s = cx_prettyquadRoot(1,0,1) gives array("i","-i"). 2) $s = cx_prettyquadRoot(1,-5,6) gives array("2","3"). 3) $s = cx_prettyquadRoot(1,2,5) gives array("-1+2i","-1-2i").
macro.gotcha: Returns strings only — not suitable for further arithmetic. No roundto parameter; precision is fixed. Use cx_quadRoot when you need numeric values for calculation, and cx_prettyquadRoot only for display.

macro.description: Returns an array of the two roots of the quadratic equation f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c. Real roots are returned as array([r1],[r2]) ordered smallest to largest; complex roots as array([Re1,Im1],[Re2,Im2]).
macro.example: 1) $roots = cx_quadRoot(1,0,1) gives array([0,1],[0,-1]) — roots of x^2+1=0 (i and -i). 2) $roots = cx_quadRoot(1,-5,6) gives array([2],[3]) — real roots. 3) $roots = cx_quadRoot(1,2,5) gives array([-1,2],[-1,-2]) — complex roots of x^2+2x+5=0.
macro.gotcha: The disp parameter produces formatted strings for display and should not be used in calculation. Real roots are stored as single-element arrays [r], not [r,0]; check root type before indexing. Use cx_prettyquadRoot for display-ready output.

macro.description: Returns all n distinct nth roots of a complex number as an array of paired values [Re, Im]. Uses De Moivre's theorem; roots are evenly spaced in angle at 2*pi/n intervals.
macro.example: 1) $r = cx_root([1,0], 2) gives array([1,0],[-1,0]) — square roots of 1. 2) $r = cx_root([0,1], 2) gives the two square roots of i. 3) $r = cx_root([1,0], 3) gives array([1,0],[Re1,Im1],[Re2,Im2]) — cube roots of unity.
macro.gotcha: Returns all n roots, not just the principal root — use cx_pow for principal root only. Results are in standard form [Re, Im]. Access individual roots by indexing: $r[0], $r[1], etc. (zero-indexed).

macro.description: Converts a complex number from standard form [Re, Im] to polar form [mod, arg]. Returns [modulus, argument] as a paired value. argin controls whether the returned argument is in radians or degrees.
macro.example: 1) $p = cx_std2pol([1,1]) gives [sqrt(2), pi/4] in radians. 2) $p = cx_std2pol([1,1], "deg") gives [sqrt(2), 45]. 3) $p = cx_std2pol([0,-3]) gives [3, -pi/2] — negative imaginary axis.
macro.gotcha: argin controls the unit of the output argument, not an input unit. Default is "rad". The argument is in the range (-pi, pi] following atan2. The reverse function is cx_pol2std.

macro.description: Returns the difference of complex numbers in standard form as [Re, Im]. The first element in num is the minuend; all subsequent elements are subtracted from it in order.
macro.example: 1) $z = cx_sub(array([5,3],[2,1])) gives [3,2] — (5+3i) - (2+i). 2) $z = cx_sub(array([2,-3],[0,-5],[sqrt(2),-1])) gives [2-sqrt(2), 3] — subtract two numbers from the first. 3) $z = cx_sub(array([1,1],[1,1])) gives [0,0].
macro.gotcha: Like cx_add, all inputs must be in standard form [Re, Im]. The first element is the minuend; elements are subtracted left to right. Passing only one element will return it unchanged.

macro.description: Approximates a decimal value as a rational fraction using continued fraction expansion. Returns an integer if d is close to a whole number, a "n/d" string in fraction format, or a "w n/d" mixed number string if format is "mixednumber" and the whole part is positive.
macro.example: 1) decimaltofraction(0.333333333) returns "1/3". 2) decimaltofraction(1.5, "mixednumber") returns "1 1/2". 3) decimaltofraction(0.142857142857) returns "1/7".
macro.gotcha: If the continued fraction expansion cannot approximate d within 1e-12 after 1000 iterations or when maxden is exceeded, the original decimal is returned as a string with its sign — always check whether the return value contains "/" before assuming a fraction was found. The default maxden is 10,000,000; cap is 1e16. Non-numeric input echoes an error and returns d.

macro.description: Formats a complex number from separate real and imaginary parts into a standard "a+bi" string. Handles special cases: imag=0 returns just the real part; imag=1 returns "real+i"; imag=-1 returns "real-i". No spaces are inserted around the + or - operator.
macro.example: 1) formatcomplex(3, 2) returns "3+2i". 2) formatcomplex(3, -2) returns "3-2i". 3) formatcomplex(5, 0) returns 5 (the real number, not a string with "+0i").
macro.gotcha: The function does not insert spaces, producing compact output like "3+2i" or "3-2i". When imag is negative (and not -1), it is concatenated directly since the negative sign is already part of the value. There is no option to use "j" instead of "i" for engineering notation. Both real and imag should be numeric — non-numeric inputs are not validated and may produce malformed output.

macro.description: Converts a fraction given as integer numerator and denominator into an English phrase. Supports options: "hyphen" (joins top and bottom with a hyphen), "mixed" (returns a mixed number if improper), "over" (returns "X over Y"), "by" (returns "X by Y"), and "literal" (skips reduction/mixed conversion). Multiple options can be combined in one string.
macro.example: 1) fractowords(3, 4) returns "three-fourths" or "three fourths" depending on phrasing. 2) fractowords(7, 2, "mixed") returns "three and one-half". 3) fractowords(1, 3, "over") returns "one over three".
macro.gotcha: Returns an empty string if numer or denom are not (near) integers, or if denom is 0. Without the "literal" option, improper fractions may be automatically reduced or converted — pass "literal" when you need the exact numerator/denominator as stated. The "over" and "by" options bypass special fraction name lookup (half, thirds, etc.) entirely.

macro.description: Reduces a fraction n/d by their GCD and returns a formatted string. Special cases: n=0 returns "0"; d=0 returns "undefined"; d=1 after reduction returns just the integer (or variable term). The dblslash parameter uses "//" instead of "/" when true. When dblslash is "parts", returns a [n, d] array of the reduced values instead of a string.
macro.example: 1) makereducedfraction(6, 4) returns "3/2". 2) makereducedfraction(6, -4) returns "-3/2" (denominator is kept positive). 3) makereducedfraction(3, 6, false, "x") returns "x/2" (numerator treated as coefficient of x).
macro.gotcha: Echoes an error and returns a raw "n/d" concatenation if either input is non-numeric. When varinnum is set and the reduced numerator is 1, the leading 1 is dropped (so the result is "x/d" not "1x/d"). Use dblslash="parts" when you need the reduced [n, d] values for further computation rather than a display string.

macro.description: Converts a number into scientific notation format. The mantissa is formatted to d decimal places (default 8). The output style is controlled by f: "x" (default) produces "m xx 10^(exp)", "" produces "m10^(exp)", and "E" produces "mEexp". Returns "0" for zero input.
macro.example: 1) makescinot(0.00045) returns "4.50000000 xx 10^(-4)". 2) makescinot(12345, 2, "") returns "1.2310^(4)". 3) makescinot(6.022e23, 3, "E") returns "6.022E23".
macro.gotcha: Echoes "makescinot needs numeric input" and returns the input unchanged if n is not numeric. When d=-1, the mantissa is rounded to 8 decimal places without number_format, which may produce varying decimal lengths. The exponent is computed as floor(log10(|n|)+1e-12) to avoid floating-point rounding errors near powers of 10.

macro.description: Cleans and normalizes an IMathAS expression string (or array of strings) using clean() and cleanbytoken(). Removes unnecessary formatting artifacts and standardizes token representation. If exp is an array, each element is cleaned individually and an array is returned.
macro.example: 1) makexxpretty("1x+0") returns a cleaned expression like "x". 2) makexxpretty(array("2x","1*y+0")) returns array("2x","y"). 3) makexxpretty($expr, array("sin","cos")) allows sin and cos as permitted function tokens.
macro.gotcha: The funcs parameter controls which function names are considered valid tokens in cleanbytoken() — omitting it uses the default empty list. This macro does not produce display-ready output (no backtick wrapping); use makexxprettydisp instead when the result will appear inline in question text.

macro.description: Like makexxpretty, cleans and normalizes an expression or array of expressions, but additionally wraps each result in backticks for inline math display. Use this when the cleaned expression will be inserted directly into question text for rendering.
macro.example: 1) makexxprettydisp("1x+0") returns a backtick-wrapped cleaned expression ready for display. 2) makexxprettydisp(array("2x","3*y")) returns each cleaned expression wrapped for display. 3) makexxprettydisp($studentExpr, array("sqrt")) cleans while allowing sqrt as a token.
macro.gotcha: If exp is an array, the return value is also an array — do not use in string concatenation without implode or similar. The backtick wrapping is for IMathAS inline math rendering; if you need the raw cleaned string for further processing, use makexxpretty instead.

macro.description: Converts a number to its English word representation. Supports negative numbers and decimals up to 9 significant digits; fractional parts are expressed using place-value words (tenths, hundredths, etc.). When addcontractiontonum is true, returns the number with its ordinal suffix (1st, 2nd, 3rd) instead of words.
macro.example: 1) numtowords(42) returns "forty-two". 2) numtowords(3.5) returns "three and five tenths". 3) numtowords(21, false, true) returns "21st".
macro.gotcha: Input is rounded to 9 decimal places before conversion, so very high-precision decimals lose accuracy. The doth parameter affects phrasing inside the convertTri() helper (e.g., inclusion of "and" between hundreds and tens) — its effect depends on the number range. For ordinal suffixes attached to digits (e.g., "21st"), set addcontractiontonum to true and the word conversion is skipped entirely.

macro.description: Formats a number (or array of numbers) to a fixed number of decimal places with optional thousands separators. Non-numeric input values are returned unchanged. Accepts and strips existing commas from values before formatting. If input is an array, returns an array.
macro.example: 1) prettyreal(1234567.5, 2) returns "1,234,567.50". 2) prettyreal(0.1234, 3) returns "0.123". 3) prettyreal(array(1000, 2000), 0, "") returns array("1000","2000") with no thousands separator.
macro.gotcha: The comma parameter defaults to "," — pass an empty string to suppress thousands separators. Non-numeric strings are returned as-is without formatting. When d is 0 (the default), decimal places are suppressed entirely; the result may differ from what number_format would produce for very large numbers due to float precision.

macro.description: Formats a number (or array of numbers) to a specified number of significant figures, with optional thousands separator, trailing-zero chopping, and automatic switch to scientific notation for very large or very small values. The special input string "DNE" is returned unchanged.
macro.example: 1) prettysigfig(12345, 3) returns "12,300". 2) prettysigfig(0.006789, 2) returns "0.0068". 3) prettysigfig(12345, 3, ",", false, true) returns scientific notation for values where |a|>1000.
macro.gotcha: When orscinot is true, any value with |a|>1000 or |a|<0.001 is delegated to makescinot(a, sigfig-1, "*") — the sigfig count passed to makescinot is one less than requested, which is intentional (sigfig-1 decimal places in the mantissa). Non-numeric strings and the value 0 are returned unchanged. Sigfig must be >= 1.

macro.description: Expands a very small number in scientific notation (e.g., 1.5E-8) into its full decimal string form (e.g., 0.000000015). Only activates when the input string contains "E" and the value is less than 0.01 in absolute value. Numbers at or above 0.01 are returned unchanged.
macro.example: 1) prettysmallnumber("1.5E-8") returns "0.000000015". 2) prettysmallnumber("2.3E-4", true) inserts thin spaces every 3 digits in the fractional part. 3) prettysmallnumber(0.5) returns 0.5 unchanged because |n| >= 0.01.
macro.gotcha: Only handles the "mantissaEexp" format — it does not handle all scientific notation styles. Numbers >= 0.01 or not containing "E" are returned completely unchanged, so this is safe to call on any numeric output. Use makescinot for the reverse operation (number to scientific notation).

macro.description: Converts a time value between units and formats it as a human-readable string. The in parameter specifies the input unit: "s" (seconds), "m" (minutes), or "h" (hours). The out parameter controls the output: "clock" for 12-hour am/pm clock format, "sclock" for clock with seconds, or a combination of "h", "m", "s" for an English phrase.
macro.example: 1) prettytime(3661, "s", "clock") returns "1:01 am". 2) prettytime(90, "m", "hm") returns "1 hour and 30 minutes". 3) prettytime(3661, "s", "sclock") returns "1:01:01 am".
macro.gotcha: For clock/sclock output, the time is first converted to seconds, then hours are taken mod 24 — times exceeding 24 hours wrap around. English phrase output (using h/m/s flags) rounds non-integer parts to 4 decimal places and pluralizes unit labels. There is no validation of the in parameter — an invalid unit silently produces wrong results.

macro.description: Adds two or more fractions and returns the reduced result. Each fraction may be a "n/d" string or a [num, den] array. If the first argument is an array, the result is returned as an array; otherwise it is returned as a string or integer.
macro.example: 1) fractionadd("1/2", "1/3") returns "5/6". 2) fractionadd([1,2], [1,3]) returns [5, 6]. 3) fractionadd("1/4", "1/4", "1/4") returns "3/4".
macro.gotcha: Requires at least 2 arguments — passing fewer echoes an error and returns "". The return type (string vs. array) depends on the type of the first argument, so be consistent across arguments if you need an array result.

macro.description: Returns an array of n proper reduced fractions with distinct denominators chosen randomly from [min, max]. Optionally sort the results by numeric value using order "inc" or "dec".
macro.example: 1) fractiondiffdrands(2, 8, 3) might return ["3/4", "1/5", "2/7"]. 2) fractiondiffdrands(2, 8, 3, "inc") returns those same fractions sorted smallest to largest.
macro.gotcha: n must not exceed the count of integers in [min, max]; if too few distinct denominators are available, diffrands will fail. order defaults to "any" (no sort).

macro.description: Returns an array of n proper reduced fractions with distinct denominators sampled without replacement from the provided list. Optionally sort results by numeric value using order "inc" or "dec".
macro.example: 1) fractiondiffdrandsfrom([3,4,5,6,8], 3) might return ["2/3", "3/8", "1/5"]. 2) fractiondiffdrandsfrom([4,6,8], 2, "dec") returns two fractions sorted largest first.
macro.gotcha: n must not exceed the length of list; if it does, diffrandsfrom will fail. order defaults to "any". Use this instead of fractiondiffdrands when you need denominators from a specific set rather than a range.

macro.description: Divides fractions left-associatively (f1 / f2 / f3 ...) and returns the reduced result. Each fraction may be a "n/d" string or a [num, den] array. Return type matches the type of the first argument.
macro.example: 1) fractiondivide("3/4", "1/2") returns "3/2". 2) fractiondivide([3,4], [1,2]) returns [3, 2]. 3) fractiondivide("1/2", "1/2", "1/2") computes (1/2 / 1/2) / 1/2 = 2.
macro.gotcha: Requires at least 2 arguments. Division is left-associative. Dividing by a fraction whose numerator reduces to 0 will produce a divide-by-zero situation — validate inputs. Return type depends on first argument type.

macro.description: Multiplies two or more fractions and returns the reduced result. Each fraction may be a "n/d" string or a [num, den] array. Return type matches the type of the first argument.
macro.example: 1) fractionmultiply("2/3", "3/4") returns "1/2". 2) fractionmultiply([2,3], [3,4]) returns [1, 2]. 3) fractionmultiply("1/2", "1/2", "1/2") returns "1/8".
macro.gotcha: Requires at least 2 arguments. Cross-cancellation does not happen before multiplication — the full product is computed then reduced. Return type depends on the first argument type.

macro.description: Returns the negation of a fraction. Input may be a "n/d" string or a [num, den] array. Return type matches the input type; the result is reduced.
macro.example: 1) fractionneg("3/4") returns "-3/4". 2) fractionneg([-1, 3]) returns [1, 3]. 3) fractionneg("2/3") returns "-2/3".
macro.gotcha: This is equivalent to multiplying by -1 and reducing. If you need to negate as part of a chain of arithmetic, passing an array input gives back an array to keep your workflow consistent.

macro.description: Parses a fraction string "a/b" or mixed number string "w a/b" and returns [numerator, denominator] as an improper fraction array. If f is already an array, it is returned as-is.
macro.example: 1) fractionparse("3/4") returns [3, 4]. 2) fractionparse("2 1/3") returns [7, 3]. 3) fractionparse([5, 6]) returns [5, 6].
macro.gotcha: A malformed string (missing numerator or denominator) returns [0, 1] and echoes an error for author accounts. This function only parses — it does not reduce. Use fractionreduce if you need a reduced result.

macro.description: Raises a fraction to the power p by computing pow(num, p) / pow(den, p), then reduces. Input may be a "n/d" string or [num, den] array. Return type matches input type.
macro.example: 1) fractionpower("2/3", 2) returns "4/9". 2) fractionpower([2,3], 3) returns [8, 27]. 3) fractionpower("3/4", 0) returns 1.
macro.gotcha: Uses PHP pow() internally. Non-integer exponents may produce floating-point numerator/denominator values that do not reduce cleanly. Negative exponents flip the fraction: fractionpower("2/3", -1) returns "3/2".

macro.description: Returns a proper reduced fraction with the given denominator. The numerator is chosen randomly in [1, denom-1] with gcd(numerator, denom) = 1. If returnval is true, returns an array [string, numeric_value] instead of just the string.
macro.example: 1) fractionrand(6) might return "5/6". 2) fractionrand(6, true) might return ["5/6", 0.8333].
macro.gotcha: denom must be >= 1; passing denom < 1 prints an error and returns "". The fraction is always proper (numerator < denominator), so fractionrand(1) will always fail since no valid numerator exists.

macro.description: Reduces a fraction to lowest terms and ensures the denominator is positive. Returns an integer if denominator reduces to 1, a "n/d" string otherwise. If retarr is true, returns [n, d] array instead.
macro.example: 1) fractionreduce("4/6") returns "2/3". 2) fractionreduce(4, 6) returns "2/3". 3) fractionreduce([4, 6], true) returns [2, 3]. 4) fractionreduce("6/3") returns 2.
macro.gotcha: Supports multiple calling conventions via variadic args: (string), (array), (num, den), or (num, den, retarr). Return type varies: check whether you need a string or array and pass retarr=true accordingly.

macro.description: Computes the nth root of a fraction and rationalizes the denominator. Delegates to radicals.php helpers: reduceradicalfrac (when rat=true) or reduceradicalfrac3 (when rat=false). Returns a string in radical-fraction form.
macro.example: 1) fractionroot("1/4") returns "1/2" (square root, rationalized). 2) fractionroot("1/3") returns "sqrt(3)/3" (rationalized form). 3) fractionroot("1/8", 3) returns the cube root in radical form.
macro.gotcha: Requires the radicals library to be loaded. The return format is whatever the underlying radicals helper produces — it is a display string, not an array. rat=true uses square-root rationalization; rat=false uses the generalized nth-root rationalization path.

macro.description: Subtracts fractions left-associatively (f1 - f2 - f3 ...) and returns the reduced result. Each fraction may be a "n/d" string or a [num, den] array. Return type matches the type of the first argument.
macro.example: 1) fractionsubtract("3/4", "1/4") returns "1/2". 2) fractionsubtract([5,6], [1,6]) returns [2, 3]. 3) fractionsubtract("1/2", "1/6", "1/6") returns "1/6".
macro.gotcha: Requires at least 2 arguments. Subtraction is left-associative: fractionsubtract(a, b, c) computes (a - b) - c, not a - (b + c). Return type depends on first argument type.

macro.description: Converts a fraction string or [num, den] array to its decimal numeric value. Returns the input unchanged if the numerator is non-numeric, and returns "" for empty input.
macro.example: 1) fractiontodecimal("3/4") returns 0.75. 2) fractiontodecimal([1, 3]) returns 0.3333... 3) fractiontodecimal("") returns "".
macro.gotcha: If denominator is 0, an error is echoed for author accounts and 0 is returned. If f is already numeric, it is returned without parsing. Avoid passing a zero denominator — validate first.

macro.description: Converts a fraction string or [num, den] array to a mixed number string. Returns an integer if denominator reduces to 1, a mixed number string "w a/b" for improper fractions, or the "a/b" string for proper fractions.
macro.example: 1) fractiontomixed([7, 3]) returns "2 1/3". 2) fractiontomixed([6, 3]) returns 2. 3) fractiontomixed([2, 5]) returns "2/5".
macro.gotcha: This function only formats — it does not reduce. If the input is not already reduced, the output will not be reduced either. Call fractionreduce first if reduction is needed. Sign normalization is applied so the denominator is always positive.

macro.description: Creates an array of answerbox placeholder strings of the form [AB#], starting at start and continuing for num entries. Use this when a multipart question needs answerboxes generated as a parallel array, especially before feeding that array into a table or layout macro such as showarrays.
macro.example: 1) ABarray(1, 4) returns array("[AB1]","[AB2]","[AB3]","[AB4]"). 2) $part2ab = ABarray(1,4) can be passed directly into showarrays("`k`",$part2kdisp,$part2inputhdr,$part2ydisp,$part2outputhdr,$part2ab) to build a table whose last column is a vertical stack of answerboxes. 3) ABarray(0,3) is useful when the first graded part in a multipart question is [AB0].
macro.gotcha: ABarray only creates placeholder strings; it does not create grading rules by itself. The generated indices must still align with the actual multipart setup in $anstypes[...] and $answer[...]. If the start index or count is wrong, the rendered question may show answerboxes that do not match the intended graded parts.

macro.signature: evalfunc(func, vars, val1, val2, ...) (alt form: evalfunc([funcExpr, varList], val1, ...))
macro.description: Evaluates a function expression at given variable values. Accepts two call forms: (1) evalfunc(funcExpr, varList, val1, ...) or (2) evalfunc([funcExpr, varList], val1, ...). If all values are numeric, returns a numeric result. If any value is non-numeric, returns an expression string with variables substituted. Returns false on validation errors.
macro.example: 1) evalfunc("x^2 + 1", "x", 3) returns 10 (numeric mode). 2) evalfunc("x + y", "x,y", 2, 5) returns 7. 3) evalfunc("x^2", "x", "a") returns "(a)^2" (string substitution mode).
macro.gotcha: Returns false (not 0 or '') on mismatched variable count, invalid variable names, or non-numeric inputs in numeric-eval mode — always check the return value. Variable names are sanitized (non-word characters stripped); empty names after sanitization cause a false return. In string-substitution mode, variables are wrapped in parentheses to reduce precedence issues, but the result is not automatically evaluated. If count(values) equals count(vars)+1, the extra trailing argument is silently ignored (internal skip-cleanup flag).

macro.description: Evaluates a numeric expression string using the IMathAS math parser (evalMathParser). Returns the numeric result, or an empty string if expr is empty/whitespace. The optional complex flag (default false) enables complex-number evaluation.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("sin(pi/2)") returns 1. 2) evalnumstr("2^10 + sqrt(4)") returns 1026. 3) evalnumstr("") returns '' (empty string).
macro.gotcha: Returns empty string '' (not 0) when expr is empty or whitespace — check for this before using the result arithmetically. Parser errors produce NaN (represented internally as sqrt(-1)). evalnumstr is a thin wrapper; the full set of supported functions (sin, cos, sqrt, etc.) is determined by the evalMathParser implementation, not by this macro itself.

macro.description: Injects a raw ASCIIsvg/AsciiMath draw command string into an existing SVG plot, immediately before the closing of the embed tag payload. Use this to add custom drawing operations not supported by the built-in macro set.
macro.example: 1) adddrawcommand($plot, "circle([0,0],2)") draws a circle of radius 2 centered at the origin. 2) adddrawcommand($plot, "line([1,1],[3,3])") draws a line segment. 3) adddrawcommand($plot, "dot([2,3],'open')") adds an open dot at (2,3).
macro.gotcha: Single quotes in cmd are automatically converted to double quotes before injection. This operates only in SVG mode — there is no text-mode fallback. The command must be valid ASCIIsvg/Asymptote syntax accepted by the graphing backend.

macro.description: Replaces numeric tick labels on an axis with fractional labels at the given step. Step may be a plain fraction like "1/2", a pi-based step like "pi/2" or "2*pi/3", or a numeric value. The axis parameter defaults to "x"; pass "y" to label the y-axis.
macro.example: 1) addfractionaxislabels($plot, "pi/2") labels the x-axis at multiples of pi/2. 2) addfractionaxislabels($plot, "1/3", "y") labels the y-axis at thirds. 3) addfractionaxislabels($plot, "2*pi/3") labels x at 0, 2pi/3, 4pi/3, 2pi.
macro.gotcha: Only works in SVG mode — the plot string must contain initPicture(...) or an error is echoed and the original plot is returned. A computed step of 0 triggers a fatal error. Non-numeric numerator/denominator after parsing also returns the original plot unchanged.

macro.description: Adds a solid inline CSS border (and optional margin) to an HTML img tag string. Border width defaults to 1px and margin defaults to 0 (not applied when 0). If the img already has a style attribute, the border/margin CSS is prepended to it.
macro.example: 1) addimageborder($img) adds a 1px solid black border. 2) addimageborder($img, 2) adds a 2px border. 3) addimageborder($img, 1, 5) adds a 1px border and 5px margin around the image.
macro.gotcha: Works only on img HTML tag strings — not on SVG embed tags from showplot/showasciisvg. The border color is always black; there is no parameter to change it. If you need to style the border color, manually wrap the image in a styled container instead.

macro.description: Adds a text label at graph-coordinate position (x, y) on an existing plot. Color defaults to black, angle defaults to 0 degrees, and size is only applied when greater than 0. In text mode, appends a description like "Label at (x,y)".
macro.example: 1) addlabel($plot, 2, 3, "A") places the label "A" at graph point (2,3) in black. 2) addlabel($plot, -1, 4, "f(x)", "red") uses red text. 3) addlabel($plot, 0, 0, "Origin", "blue", "", 45, 12) rotates the label 45 degrees at font size 12.
macro.gotcha: Coordinates are in graph (data) units, not pixels — use addlabelabs for pixel-based placement. Quotes inside the label string are escaped automatically in SVG mode. The loc parameter is a backend-specific placement code (e.g., "above", "right") and may have no effect in text mode.

macro.description: Adds a text label at absolute pixel coordinates (x, y) on an existing plot. Unlike addlabel, coordinates are in pixels measured from the image origin, not in graph data units. Useful for placing annotations at fixed positions regardless of axis range.
macro.example: 1) addlabelabs($plot, 50, 100, "Note") places label "Note" at pixel (50,100). 2) addlabelabs($plot, 10, 10, "Origin", "blue") uses blue text. 3) addlabelabs($plot, 150, 20, "Max", "red", "above", 0) places with location hint.
macro.gotcha: Use this only when you need pixel-exact placement; for data-coordinate placement use addlabel instead. The function accepts optional args 5-7 via func_get_arg internally, so passing them positionally is required. In text mode, appends a description mentioning pixel coordinates.

macro.description: Updates the setBorder() margins in an SVG plot string to create whitespace padding around the graph area. Left is required; bottom, right, and top all default to 5. Useful for making room for axis labels or annotations near the edge.
macro.example: 1) addplotborder($plot, 30) adds a 30px left border and 5px on the other three sides. 2) addplotborder($plot, 40, 20, 10, 10) sets all four borders explicitly. 3) addplotborder($plot, 30, 5, 5, 20) adds extra top margin for a title.
macro.gotcha: Only works in SVG mode and only modifies an existing setBorder(...) call — if the plot string does not contain setBorder, the function makes no change. Ensure you call showplot or showasciisvg before this function.

macro.description: Converts parallel x and y coordinate arrays into an array of plot command strings for filled dots. Each command is in the format "dot,x,y,closed,color" and can be passed directly to showplot as part of a funcs array. Color defaults to blue.
macro.example: 1) showplot(arraystodoteqns(array(1,2,3), array(4,5,6))) plots three blue filled dots. 2) arraystodoteqns($xvals, $yvals, "red") generates red dot commands. 3) showplot(array_merge(arraystodoteqns($x, $y), array("x+1"))) overlays dots and a line.
macro.gotcha: Returns an empty array with an error if either input is not an array, or if any element is itself an array. If xArray and yArray have different lengths, a warning is echoed and the function continues using only indices where a y value exists. Use arraystodots for plain "x,y" coordinate strings instead of dot commands.

macro.description: Converts parallel x and y coordinate arrays into an array of plain "x,y" coordinate strings. The result is typically used as input to connectthedots or similar functions that expect coordinate pairs, not as direct showplot funcs arguments.
macro.example: 1) arraystodots(array(0,1,2), array(0,1,4)) returns array("0,0","1,1","2,4"). 2) connectthedots is commonly called with the output of arraystodots. 3) arraystodots($x, $y) where $x and $y come from randomized arrays.
macro.gotcha: Does not check that xArray and yArray have the same length — it iterates over count(xArray) and indexes yArray at the same position, which may produce PHP notices if yArray is shorter. Returns an empty array with an error if either input is not an array or contains array elements.

macro.description: Updates the width (and optionally height) attributes of an HTML img tag string. Existing width/height attributes and any CSS width/height style declarations are removed first before the new attributes are injected.
macro.example: 1) changeimagesize($img, 300) sets the image width to 300px with no explicit height. 2) changeimagesize($img, 400, 250) sets both width to 400px and height to 250px. 3) changeimagesize(textonimage($url, $label, 10, 10), 200) can be chained with other image macros.
macro.gotcha: If h is omitted or empty, no height attribute is added, which lets the browser scale height proportionally. The w argument is cast to int (sanitized), so passing a string like "300px" will be coerced. This works only on img HTML tag strings, not on SVG embed tags produced by showplot.

macro.description: Generates an array of parametric line segment plot commands connecting consecutive (x,y) points. The result is passed as part of the funcs array to showplot. Supports open/closed endpoint markers via startdot and enddot, and handles vertical segments correctly.
macro.example: 1) showplot(connectthedots(array(0,1,2,3), array(0,1,0,1))) draws a zigzag line. 2) connectthedots($x, $y, "red", 2, "open", "closed") draws a thick red piecewise line with an open start dot and closed end dot. 3) connectthedots($x, $y, "blue") uses blue color with default thickness 1.
macro.gotcha: Returns an empty array with an error if xArray and yArray are not equal-length arrays — unlike arraystodots, length mismatch is a fatal error here. Vertical segments (equal consecutive x values) are handled with a special vertical-line command format. The startdot/enddot values are only inserted on the very first and very last segments respectively.

macro.description: Renders header/row pairs as a horizontal HTML stats table where each pair becomes one table row. The optional trailing arg sets body cell alignment (single char: c/r/l) or accepts an opts object. Shorter rows are padded with empty cells to match the longest row.
macro.example: 1) horizshowarrays("Scores", array(85,90,78), "Grades", array("B","A","C")) produces a 2-row table. 2) horizshowarrays("Values", $vals, "c") centers all data cells. 3) Pass opts array(caption=>"My Table", tablealign=>"center") as the trailing arg for a centered captioned table.
macro.gotcha: Returns false if fewer than 2 arguments are given. Unlike showarrays, the format string applies a single alignment to all data cells, not per-column. Non-array row values are parsed via listtoarray().

macro.description: Combines two or more plot strings (from showplot or showasciisvg) into a single plot by merging their drawing commands. In SVG mode, drawing commands from all plots after the first are extracted and injected into the first plot. In text mode, subsequent plot headers are stripped and text is concatenated.
macro.example: 1) mergeplots(showplot(array("x"), -5, 5), showplot(array("x^2"), -5, 5)) overlays a line and a parabola. 2) mergeplots($p1, $p2, $p3) merges three plots into one. 3) With a single argument, mergeplots($plot) returns the plot unchanged.
macro.gotcha: All input plots should use the same axis bounds and image size — mergeplots does not reconcile differing initPicture() settings; only commands from plots 2..N are extracted, not their viewport. Text mode strips only the leading "Graphs ..." header from subsequent plots.

macro.description: Replaces or adds the alt attribute on an SVG plot embed tag with the provided alttext. In text mode (graphdisp==0), discards the plot entirely and returns alttext directly. Use this to provide meaningful accessibility descriptions for generated graphs.
macro.example: 1) replacealttext($plot, "A parabola opening upward with vertex at the origin.") sets a descriptive alt text. 2) replacealttext($plot, "Line graph showing increasing trend from 2010 to 2020.") replaces a previously auto-generated alt. 3) In text mode, replacealttext($plot, "Graph description here") returns just the description string.
macro.gotcha: In SVG mode, if the plot already has an alt="..." attribute it is replaced; if absent, the attribute is added. The alt text is encoded for display before injection. In text mode the plot string is completely ignored — only alttext is returned.

macro.description: Renders parallel arrays as a vertical HTML stats table. Each header/column pair becomes one table column. Accepts an optional trailing format string (alignment per column: c/r/l) or an opts object with keys align, caption, and tablealign.
macro.example: 1) showarrays("x", array(1,2,3), "y", array(4,5,6)) produces a 2-column table with headers x and y. 2) showarrays("Name", $names, "Score", $scores, "rl") right-aligns the Name column and left-aligns Score. 3) showarrays(array("x","y"), array(array(1,2,3),array(4,5,6))) uses the alternate 2-arg array-of-arrays syntax.
macro.gotcha: Returns false (not an empty string) if fewer than 2 arguments are given. Column headers must be scalars — passing an array as a header triggers a warning and replaces it with an empty string. Cell values are output unescaped, so HTML in data renders as markup.

macro.description: Renders a raw ASCIIsvg script as an SVG embed element. Line breaks in the script are converted to semicolons, and both line and block comments are removed before embedding. Width and height default to 200px. If alt is null, an auto-generated alt based on the script content is used.
macro.example: 1) showasciisvg("initPicture(-5,5,-5,5); axes(); path([[0,0],[3,4]],'blue')") renders a custom path. 2) showasciisvg($script, 300, 300, "A triangle with vertices at (0,0), (3,0), and (1,2).") sets a custom size and alt. 3) In text mode, showasciisvg($script) returns the alt text only.
macro.gotcha: Passing an array as the second argument triggers a warning and resets width/height to 200 and alt to empty. In text mode, only alt text is returned — the script is not executed. Auto-generated alt text is the literal script string wrapped in brackets, which is rarely useful; always provide a meaningful alt string for accessibility.

macro.description: Displays a flat 1D array as an HTML table (or preformatted text) arranged into rows of n columns. Useful for showing a dataset without explicit column headers. The opts arg accepts the string "pre" for preformatted output, an alignment string, or an object with keys format, align, caption, and tablealign.
macro.example: 1) showdataarray(array(1,2,3,4,5,6), 3) displays values in a 3-column table. 2) showdataarray($data, 5, "c") centers values in 5 columns. 3) showdataarray($data, 4, "pre") outputs values in fixed-width preformatted text.
macro.gotcha: Returns an empty string (not false) if input is not an array. In pre mode, values are padded to the maximum string width of any element, so very long values widen all cells.

macro.description: Generates an SVG or text plot from one or more function/point specifications. Returns an embed tag (SVG mode) or a textual description (text mode) depending on the session graphdisp setting. Default axis range is -5 to 5 on both axes; default image size is 200x200 pixels.
macro.example: 1) showplot(array("x^2"), -3, 3, 0, 9) plots y=x^2 from x=-3 to x=3. 2) showplot($funcs, "0:0", 10, "0:0", 10) uses the 0: prefix to enforce first-quadrant-only display. 3) showplot($funcs, -5, 5, "auto:-10", "auto:10") enables auto-scaling with fallback bounds.
macro.gotcha: Passing a non-scalar optional argument echoes an "Invalid input k to showplot" warning and keeps the default for that setting. The plotting grammar for the funcs parameter is backend-specific — consult the graphing backend docs for supported equation/point formats.

macro.description: Renders a 2D rectangular matrix as an HTML stats table with row and column header labels. The optional fourth arg is either an alignment string (c/r/l/default) or an opts object with keys caption, align, and tablealign.
macro.example: 1) showrecttable(array(array(1,2),array(3,4)), array("Col A","Col B"), array("Row 1","Row 2")) produces a 2x2 labeled table. 2) Pass "r" as the fourth arg to right-align all data cells. 3) Pass array(caption=>"Frequency Table", tablealign=>"center") for a centered captioned table.
macro.gotcha: Returns an error string if row or column label counts do not match matrix dimensions — always verify dimensions before calling. Known quirk: when opts is an array and opts["format"] is set, the implementation reads opts["align"] instead (likely a typo); use opts["align"] to control alignment reliably.

macro.signature: textonimage(imgOrUrl, text1, left1, top1, [text2, left2, top2, ...])
macro.description: Overlays one or more text/HTML elements at absolute pixel positions on top of an image. The image can be provided as an img tag string or as an http URL (which is wrapped into an img tag automatically). Returns an HTML container with absolutely positioned overlays.
macro.example: 1) textonimage($img, "Label A", 50, 30) overlays "Label A" at pixel (50,30). 2) textonimage("https://example.com/img.png", "x", 100, 80, "y", 200, 80) overlays two labels on an external image. 3) textonimage($img, "[AB:1]", 120, 60) overlays an answer box at (120,60).
macro.gotcha: Overlay items are processed in groups of 3 (text, left, top); extra trailing arguments are silently ignored. Text not containing answer box tokens (like [AB:1]) is marked aria-hidden and omitted in text mode — for accessible content, embed answer boxes or use replacealttext.

macro.signature: ineqbetweenplot(funcstring, [xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, labels, grid, width, height])
macro.description: Graphs one or more functions and shades the single region that simultaneously satisfies all above/below constraints — i.e., the intersection of all the individual half-planes. Also supports vertical lines using x=number with filltype right or left. funcstring entry format: function of x, above or below, linecolor, dash, strokewidth, fillcolor — or x=number, right or left, linecolor, dash, strokewidth, fillcolor.
macro.example: 1) ineqbetweenplot(["x+1,above", "x^2,below"]) — shades only the region both above y=x+1 and below y=x^2. 2) ineqbetweenplot(["x=2,right", "x=5,left"]) — shades the vertical strip between x=2 and x=5. 3) ineqbetweenplot(["x+1,above,blue", "2*x-3,below,red"], -5, 5, -5, 5) — two-constraint region with custom line colors and axis bounds.
macro.gotcha: Unlike ineqplot, this function shades the intersection of all constraints rather than each region independently — use ineqplot when you want separate shading per curve. The funcstring field order differs slightly from ineqplot: linecolor comes before fillcolor here. Vertical line constraints use the x=number syntax with right or left as filltype, which is only supported in ineqbetweenplot, not ineqplot.

macro.signature: ineqplot(funcstring, [xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, labels, grid, width, height])
macro.description: Graphs one or more functions and shades above or below each curve independently according to the funcstring specification. Each function entry specifies: function of x, filltype (above or below), fillcolor, linecolor, dash, strokewidth. funcstring can be a single string or an array of strings.
macro.example: 1) ineqplot("x+1,above") — graphs y=x+1 and shades the region above it with default colors. 2) ineqplot(["x^2,below,blue,red", "x+1,above,green,black"]) — graphs two curves with individual fill and line colors. 3) ineqplot("2*x-1,above,yellow,blue", -5, 5, -5, 5) — uses custom axis bounds.
macro.gotcha: Function and filltype are the only required fields in each funcstring entry — fillcolor, linecolor, dash, and strokewidth are optional and positional. filltype must be exactly "above" or "below". For problems that shade the intersection region satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously, use ineqbetweenplot instead. The optional axis/display parameters follow the funcstring as positional arguments in a fixed order.

macro.description: Returns the absolute value of v. In complex mode, returns the magnitude. Provided by the expression parser.
macro.example: 1) abs(-5) returns 5. 2) abs(3.7) returns 3.7. 3) evalnumstr("abs(-pi)") returns approximately 3.1416.
macro.gotcha: In complex mode, abs returns the modulus (magnitude), not just the real part. For real mode, negative inputs return their positive counterpart with no issue.

macro.description: Returns the inverse cosine of v in radians. Result is in the range [0, pi]. Provided by the expression parser. Returns NaN if v is outside [-1, 1] in real mode.
macro.example: 1) arccos(1) returns 0. 2) arccos(0) returns pi/2 (approximately 1.5708). 3) evalnumstr("arccos(-1)") returns pi (approximately 3.1416).
macro.gotcha: Domain is [-1, 1]; values outside this range return NaN in real mode. Do not use acos() — this parser uses arccos().

macro.description: Returns the inverse sine of v in radians. Result is in the range [-pi/2, pi/2]. Provided by the expression parser. Returns NaN if v is outside [-1, 1] in real mode.
macro.example: 1) arcsin(0) returns 0. 2) arcsin(1) returns pi/2 (approximately 1.5708). 3) evalnumstr("arcsin(0.5)") returns approximately 0.5236.
macro.gotcha: Domain is [-1, 1]; values outside this range return NaN in real mode. Do not use asin() — this parser uses arcsin().

macro.description: Returns the inverse tangent of v in radians. Result is in the range (-pi/2, pi/2). Provided by the expression parser. Defined for all real v.
macro.example: 1) arctan(0) returns 0. 2) arctan(1) returns pi/4 (approximately 0.7854). 3) evalnumstr("arctan(-1)") returns approximately -0.7854.
macro.gotcha: Unlike arcsin/arccos, arctan has no domain restriction for real inputs. Do not use atan() — this parser uses arctan(). For atan2 behaviour, arctan is single-argument only.

macro.description: Returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to x (round up). Provided by the expression parser (mathphp2.php). Availability depends on the parser's allowed function list.
macro.example: 1) ceil(3.1) returns 4. 2) ceil(-2.9) returns -2. 3) evalnumstr("ceil(pi)") returns 4.
macro.gotcha: For negative values, ceil rounds toward zero (e.g., ceil(-2.9) = -2, not -3). Ensure ceil is included in the parser's allowed function list for your IMathAS configuration.

macro.description: Returns the cosine of t, where t is an angle in radians. Provided by the expression parser via evalnumstr/evalMathParser. Returns NaN for invalid inputs in real mode.
macro.example: 1) cos(0) returns 1. 2) cos(pi) returns -1. 3) evalnumstr("cos(pi/3)") returns 0.5.
macro.gotcha: Input must be in radians. For invalid parse/eval, returns NaN (sqrt(-1) sentinel). Do not confuse with PHP built-in cos() — this is the parser-level function.

macro.description: Returns the cotangent of t (cos(t)/sin(t)), where t is in radians. Provided by the expression parser. Returns NaN for invalid inputs or where sin(t) = 0.
macro.example: 1) cot(pi/4) returns 1. 2) cot(pi/3) returns approximately 0.577. 3) evalnumstr("cot(pi/6)") returns approximately 1.732.
macro.gotcha: Undefined where sin(t) = 0 (t = 0, pi, etc.); returns NaN at those points. Input must be in radians.

macro.description: Returns the cosecant of t (1/sin(t)), where t is in radians. Provided by the expression parser. Returns NaN for invalid inputs or where sin(t) = 0.
macro.example: 1) csc(pi/2) returns 1. 2) csc(pi/6) returns 2. 3) evalnumstr("csc(pi/4)") returns approximately 1.414.
macro.gotcha: Undefined wherever sin(t) = 0 (i.e., t = 0, pi, 2*pi, etc.); parser returns NaN at those points. Input must be in radians.

macro.description: Mathematical constant e (Euler's number, approximately 2.71828182845905). Provided as a named constant by the expression parser (mathparser.php/mathphp2.php). No arguments.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("e") returns approximately 2.71828. 2) evalnumstr("e^2") returns approximately 7.389. 3) evalnumstr("ln(e)") returns 1.
macro.gotcha: e is a constant, not a function — do not write e(). Only available inside expression strings passed to evalnumstr or evalMathParser. Do not confuse with PHP's M_E constant, which is not directly accessible in expression strings.

macro.description: Returns the factorial of v. Intended for nonnegative integers. Supported as a postfix operator (v!) and as a named function. Provided by the expression parser (mathphp2.php).
macro.example: 1) factorial(5) returns 120. 2) 6! returns 720 (postfix form in expressions). 3) evalnumstr("4!") returns 24.
macro.gotcha: Defined reliably only for nonnegative integers. Behaviour for non-integers or negative values is implementation-defined and may return NaN. The postfix form v! is rewritten internally by the parser to a factorial node.

macro.description: Returns the largest integer less than or equal to x (round down). Provided by the expression parser (mathphp2.php). Availability depends on the parser's allowed function list.
macro.example: 1) floor(3.9) returns 3. 2) floor(-2.1) returns -3. 3) evalnumstr("floor(pi)") returns 3.
macro.gotcha: For negative values, floor rounds toward negative infinity (e.g., floor(-2.1) = -3, not -2). Ensure floor is included in the parser's allowed function list for your IMathAS configuration.

macro.description: Returns the floating-point remainder of a divided by b. This is the expression-parser version of modulo, exposed via macros.php and usable inside evalnumstr strings.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("fmod(10.5, 3)") returns 1.5. 2) evalnumstr("fmod(7, 2.5)") returns 2. 3) fmod(10, 3) returns 1 (in PHP macro context).
macro.gotcha: Prefer fmod() over mod() when working inside expression strings (evalnumstr). For division by zero (b=0), returns NaN. Results for negative operands follow C-style fmod semantics (sign follows dividend).

macro.description: Returns the greatest common divisor of two or more integers using the Euclidean algorithm. Accepts any number of arguments — the result is the GCD of all inputs combined. Commonly used to verify coprimality or reduce fractions to lowest terms.
macro.example: 1) gcd(12, 8) returns 4. 2) gcd(12, 8, 6) returns 2. 3) gcd(7, 13) returns 1 (coprime). 4) gcd($num, $den) == 1 checks if a fraction is already in lowest terms.
macro.gotcha: Both inputs are treated as integers — non-integer inputs are truncated. gcd(0, n) returns n (by convention). gcd(0, 0) returns 0. Does not simplify fractions automatically — use the result to divide numerator and denominator separately.

macro.description: Returns the maximum value among all provided arguments. Accepts two or more numeric arguments. Provided by the expression parser (mathphp2.php).
macro.example: 1) max(3, 7) returns 7. 2) max(5, 2, 8, 1) returns 8. 3) evalnumstr("max(pi, 3.0)") returns approximately 3.1416.
macro.gotcha: Availability depends on the parser's allowed function list. Passing a single argument or non-numeric arguments may return NaN. Do not confuse with PHP's built-in max() — this operates within expression parser context.

macro.description: Returns the minimum value among all provided arguments. Accepts two or more numeric arguments. Provided by the expression parser (mathphp2.php).
macro.example: 1) min(3, 7) returns 3. 2) min(5, 2, 8, 1) returns 1. 3) evalnumstr("min(pi, 3.2)") returns approximately 3.1416.
macro.gotcha: Availability depends on the parser's allowed function list. Passing a single argument or non-numeric arguments may return NaN. Do not confuse with PHP's built-in min() — this operates within expression parser context.

macro.description: Returns a modulo b. This is a PHP-level macro defined in math.php, used when you need modulo outside the expression-parser context.
macro.example: 1) mod(10, 3) returns 1. 2) mod(7, 2) returns 1. 3) mod(15, 5) returns 0.
macro.gotcha: Division by zero (b=0) is implementation-defined and may return NaN or cause an error. Behaviour for negative operands may differ from PHP's % operator — test edge cases. Use fmod() inside expression strings instead if working within evalnumstr.

macro.description: Addition operator wrapper used by the expression parser (precedence 10, left-associative). Represents the + operator in calconarray and array-math contexts within IMathAS expressions.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("3 + 4") returns 7. 2) In calconarray context, op_add combines two array-element values. 3) evalnumstr("x + 2") with x=5 returns 7.
macro.gotcha: This is the parser-internal representation of +; you do not call op_add() directly in IMathAS question code — write a + b in expression strings instead. Invalid operands produce NaN.

macro.description: Division operator wrapper used by the expression parser (precedence 20, left-associative). Represents the / operator in calconarray and array-math contexts within IMathAS expressions.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("10 / 4") returns 2.5. 2) evalnumstr("pi / 2") returns approximately 1.5708. 3) In calconarray context, op_div divides two array-element values.
macro.gotcha: Division by zero (b=0) produces NaN, not a PHP error. This is the parser-internal representation of /; do not call op_div() directly in question code.

macro.description: Multiplication operator wrapper used by the expression parser (precedence 20, left-associative). Represents the * operator in calconarray and array-math contexts within IMathAS expressions.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("4 5") returns 20. 2) evalnumstr("2 pi") returns approximately 6.2832. 3) In calconarray context, op_mul multiplies two array-element values.
macro.gotcha: This is the parser-internal representation of *; do not call op_mul() directly. Higher precedence than op_add/op_sub (20 vs 10). Invalid operands produce NaN.

macro.description: Unary negation operator wrapper used by the expression parser (precedence 40, right-associative). Represents the unary - operator in calconarray and array-math contexts within IMathAS expressions.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("-5") returns -5. 2) evalnumstr("-pi") returns approximately -3.1416. 3) evalnumstr("-(3+2)") returns -5.
macro.gotcha: Distinct from op_sub (binary minus). Has the highest precedence among the operator wrappers (40). Do not call op_neg() directly — write -a in expression strings. Invalid operands produce NaN.

macro.description: Exponentiation operator wrapper used by the expression parser (precedence 30, right-associative). Represents the ^ operator in calconarray and array-math contexts within IMathAS expressions.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("2^10") returns 1024. 2) evalnumstr("e^1") returns approximately 2.7183. 3) evalnumstr("4^0.5") returns 2.
macro.gotcha: Right-associative: a^b^c is evaluated as a^(b^c). For negative base with non-integer exponent in real mode, may return NaN. Do not call op_pow() directly — use ^ in expression strings.

macro.description: Subtraction operator wrapper used by the expression parser (precedence 10, left-associative). Represents the - binary operator in calconarray and array-math contexts within IMathAS expressions.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("10 - 3") returns 7. 2) evalnumstr("pi - 1") returns approximately 2.1416. 3) In calconarray context, op_sub subtracts two array-element values.
macro.gotcha: This is the parser-internal representation of binary -; do not call op_sub() directly. For unary negation, see op_neg. Invalid operands produce NaN.

macro.description: Mathematical constant pi (approximately 3.14159265358979). Provided as a named constant by the expression parser (mathparser.php/mathphp2.php). No arguments.
macro.example: 1) evalnumstr("pi") returns approximately 3.14159. 2) evalnumstr("2*pi") returns approximately 6.28318. 3) evalnumstr("sin(pi/2)") returns 1.
macro.gotcha: pi is a constant, not a function — do not write pi(). It is only available inside expression strings passed to evalnumstr or evalMathParser, not as a standalone IMathAS PHP variable.

macro.description: Rounds x to the nearest integer, or to digits decimal places if specified. Provided by the expression parser (mathphp2.php). Availability depends on the parser's allowed function list.
macro.example: 1) round(3.7) returns 4. 2) round(3.14159, 2) returns 3.14. 3) evalnumstr("round(2.5)") returns 3.
macro.gotcha: The digits parameter support depends on parser configuration and may not be available in all IMathAS setups. Half-way rounding (e.g., 0.5) follows PHP rounding rules (rounds away from zero).

macro.description: Returns the secant of t (1/cos(t)), where t is in radians. Provided by the expression parser. Returns NaN for invalid inputs or where cos(t) = 0.
macro.example: 1) sec(0) returns 1. 2) sec(pi/3) returns 2. 3) evalnumstr("sec(pi/4)") returns approximately 1.414.
macro.gotcha: Undefined wherever cos(t) = 0 (i.e., t = pi/2 + n*pi); parser returns NaN at those points. Input must be in radians.

macro.description: Returns the sign of a: typically -1 for negative, 0 for zero, and 1 for positive. The optional second argument controls behaviour near zero; exact semantics depend on parser configuration.
macro.example: 1) sign(-7) returns -1. 2) sign(0) returns 0. 3) sign(3.5) returns 1.
macro.gotcha: Behaviour near zero (including the effect of the optional option argument) is parser-defined and may vary across IMathAS versions. Do not rely on sign(0) returning exactly 0 without testing.

macro.description: Returns the sine of t, where t is an angle in radians. Provided by the expression parser via evalnumstr/evalMathParser. Returns NaN for invalid inputs in real mode.
macro.example: 1) sin(0) returns 0. 2) sin(pi/2) returns 1. 3) evalnumstr("sin(pi/6)") returns 0.5.
macro.gotcha: Input must be in radians, not degrees. For invalid parse/eval, returns NaN (sqrt(-1) sentinel). Complex-mode behaviour depends on parser configuration.

macro.description: Returns the square root of x. In real mode, x must be >= 0; negative inputs produce NaN. Provided by the expression parser (mathphp2.php).
macro.example: 1) sqrt(9) returns 3. 2) sqrt(2) returns approximately 1.4142. 3) evalnumstr("sqrt(pi)") returns approximately 1.7725.
macro.gotcha: sqrt(-1) is used internally by the parser as the NaN sentinel value, so negative inputs in real mode return this NaN marker. In complex mode, sqrt of a negative may return a complex number.

macro.description: Returns the tangent of t, where t is an angle in radians. Provided by the expression parser via evalnumstr/evalMathParser. Returns NaN for invalid inputs or undefined points.
macro.example: 1) tan(0) returns 0. 2) tan(pi/4) returns 1. 3) evalnumstr("tan(pi/3)") returns approximately 1.732.
macro.gotcha: tan is undefined at pi/2 + n*pi; the parser may return NaN or a very large number at those points. Input must be in radians.

macro.description: Determines whether a plain array (not a matrix) is the zero vector, i.e., all entries are zero. Returns true if all entries are zero, false otherwise.
macro.example: 1) arrayIsZeroVector(array(0,0,0)) returns true. 2) arrayIsZeroVector(array(0,1,0)) returns false. 3) arrayIsZeroVector(matrixgetcol($A, 0, true)) checks if the first column is zero.
macro.gotcha: The input must be a plain array, not a matrix object. Use matrixgetrow() or matrixgetcol() with asArray=true to convert a matrix row or column before passing it here. Returns a boolean.
