macro.description: Creates a new matrix item from a flat array of values in row-major order (R1C1, R1C2, ..., R2C1, ...). Use matrixformat() to convert the result to an ASCIIMath string for display or as an $answer.
macro.example: 1) matrix(array(1,2,3,4), 2, 2) creates a 2x2 matrix. 2) matrix(array(3/2, 2^3, 5+1, 3), 2, 2) uses calculated values. 3) $A = matrix(array(1,0,0,1), 2, 2) creates a 2x2 identity.
macro.gotcha: vals must be a flat array in row-major order, not an array of arrays. Dimensions rows and cols must match the length of vals exactly or the matrix will be malformed.

macro.description: Tests whether the rows of matrix A form a basis for the row space of matrix B. Returns true if rows of A both span the row space of B and are linearly independent.
macro.example: 1) matrixAbasisForB($stumatrix, $answer) checks if the student supplied a correct basis. 2) Equivalent to matrixAspansB(A,B) and matrixIsRowsLinInd(A) both being true.
macro.gotcha: A must span the row space of B (same as matrixAspansB) AND the rows of A must be linearly independent. Returns a boolean. Useful for grading basis problems.

macro.description: Tests whether the rows of matrix A span the row space of matrix B. Returns true if every row of B is a linear combination of the rows of A.
macro.example: 1) matrixAspansB($stumatrix, $answer) checks if the student's set of vectors spans the same row space as the answer.
macro.gotcha: This tests spanning only — rows of A may be linearly dependent. To test for a basis (spanning and independent), use matrixAbasisForB() instead. Returns a boolean.

macro.description: Tests whether the linear system Ax = b has at least one solution. A is the coefficient matrix and b is an m x 1 column matrix. Returns true if a solution exists, false otherwise.
macro.example: 1) matrixAxbHasSolution($A, $b) returns true if Ax=b is consistent. 2) Use in answer-checking to verify that a student's b vector is in the column space of A.
macro.gotcha: b must be an m x 1 matrix (a column matrix), not a plain array. Returns a boolean. The function does not return the solution; use matrixsolve() for that.

macro.description: Compares test matrix to correct matrix entry-by-entry and returns true if they are equivalent within the given tolerance. Default tolerance is relative 0.001. Prefix tol with '\|' for absolute tolerance.
macro.example: 1) matrixCompare($stumatrix, $answer) checks with default relative tolerance. 2) matrixCompare($stumatrix, $answer, 0.01) uses relative tolerance 0.01. 3) matrixCompare($stumatrix, $answer, "\|0.001") uses absolute tolerance.
macro.gotcha: Returns true or false. Default tolerance is relative (0.001). For absolute tolerance prefix the value with '\|'. Dimensions of test and correct must match or the function returns false.

macro.description: Computes and returns the determinant of square matrix m as a scalar.
macro.example: 1) matrixDet($A) returns the determinant of A. 2) if (matrixDet($A) != 0) — checks if A is invertible. 3) matrixDet(matrixGetMinor($A, 0, 1)) computes the (0,1) minor determinant.
macro.gotcha: m must be a square matrix. For very large matrices or those with floating-point entries, the result may have small floating-point errors. The HTML reference shows the function as det(matrix) but the correct macro name is matrixDet.

macro.description: Given an array of eigenvalues (repeated per multiplicity) and a matrix of corresponding eigenvectors (as columns), constructs and returns the matrix PDP^-1, i.e., reconstructs the original diagonalizable matrix.
macro.example: 1) $pair = matrixFromEigenvals(array(2,3)); $A = matrixFormMatrixFromEigValEigVec($pair[0], $pair[1]); reconstructs the matrix.
macro.gotcha: Eigenvalues must be listed with multiplicity. The eigenvectors matrix must have eigenvectors as columns in the same order as the eigenvalues. Intended for use with matrixFromEigenvals() output.

macro.description: Takes an array of eigenvectors in the format returned by matrixFromEigenvals() and returns an array of ASCIIMath strings, one per eigenvector. Complex elements are given as [real, imag] arrays; complex conjugate pairs are auto-generated.
macro.example: 1) $strs = matrixFormatEigenvecs($pair[1]); $strs[0] displays the first eigenvector. 2) matrixFormatEigenvecs(array(array(1,2,3), array(array(1,3),array(4,5),2))) formats real and complex eigenvectors.
macro.gotcha: Input format must match exactly what matrixFromEigenvals() returns. Complex elements within an eigenvector must be [real, imag] arrays. Only one of each complex conjugate pair should be listed; the conjugate is generated automatically.

macro.description: Creates a matrix by assembling the given column vectors side by side. Each column can be either an n x 1 column matrix or a plain array.
macro.example: 1) matrixFromCols($v1, $v2, $v3) creates a matrix whose columns are v1, v2, v3. 2) matrixFromCols(array(1,0), array(0,1)) creates a 2x2 identity.
macro.gotcha: All columns must have the same number of rows. Columns can be nx1 matrix objects or plain arrays — both are accepted.

macro.description: Generates a matrix with integer entries and a corresponding set of eigenvectors, given an array of desired eigenvalues. Complex eigenvalues are specified as [real, imag] for one of each conjugate pair. Returns array(matrix, eigenvectors) where eigenvectors is an array of arrays.
macro.example: 1) $pair = matrixFromEigenvals(array(2, 3)); $A = $pair[0]; $evecs = $pair[1]; 2) $pair = matrixFromEigenvals(array(array(1,2), 3)); handles complex eigenvalue 1+2i.
macro.gotcha: For complex eigenvalues, supply only one of the conjugate pair as [real, imag]. The eigenvectors output has complex elements also as [real, imag] arrays. Use matrixFormatEigenvecs() to display them and matrixFormMatrixFromEigValEigVec() to reconstruct the matrix.

macro.description: Creates a matrix by stacking the given row vectors. Each row can be either a 1 x n row matrix or a plain array.
macro.example: 1) matrixFromRows($r1, $r2, $r3) creates a matrix whose rows are r1, r2, r3. 2) matrixFromRows(array(1,2), array(3,4)) creates the matrix [[1,2],[3,4]].
macro.gotcha: All rows must have the same number of columns. Rows can be 1xn matrix objects or plain arrays — both are accepted.

macro.description: Returns a matrix whose columns form a basis for the column space of matrix m. The column space basis is derived from the pivot columns of m.
macro.example: 1) matrixGetColumnSpace($A) returns a basis matrix for the column space of A. 2) Use matrixformat(matrixtranspose(matrixGetColumnSpace($A))) to display the basis as rows.
macro.gotcha: The returned matrix may have fewer columns than the original. The column space equals the range (image) of the linear transformation defined by A.

macro.description: Returns the (n-1) x (n-1) submatrix obtained by deleting row rowNo and column colNo from square matrix m. Used to compute determinants by cofactor expansion.
macro.example: 1) matrixGetMinor($A, 0, 0) removes the first row and first column. 2) matrixDet(matrixGetMinor($A, 1, 2)) gives the minor determinant for cofactor (1,2).
macro.gotcha: Only works for square matrices. rowNo and colNo are 0-indexed. The result is a matrix one size smaller in each dimension.

macro.description: Returns the rank of matrix m as an integer, defined as the number of linearly independent rows (equivalently columns) of m.
macro.example: 1) matrixGetRank($A) returns the rank of A. 2) if (matrixGetRank($A) == matrixNumberOfRows($A)) — checks if rows are linearly independent.
macro.gotcha: The rank is computed via row reduction internally. For large or near-singular matrices floating-point precision may affect the result.

macro.description: Returns a matrix whose rows form a basis for the row space of matrix m. The basis is obtained by row-reducing m and keeping the nonzero rows.
macro.example: 1) matrixGetRowSpace($A) returns a basis matrix for the row space of A. 2) matrixformat(matrixGetRowSpace($A)) formats the basis for display.
macro.gotcha: The returned matrix may have fewer rows than the original if m has linearly dependent rows. Use matrixAspansB() or matrixAbasisForB() to compare against student answers.

macro.description: Tests whether the column vectors of matrix m are linearly independent. Returns true if they are linearly independent, false if linearly dependent.
macro.example: 1) matrixIsColsLinInd($A) returns true if columns are linearly independent. 2) Equivalent to checking if rank equals number of columns.
macro.gotcha: Returns a boolean true or false. Column linear independence is equivalent to the null space of A being trivial.

macro.description: Tests whether a given real number is an eigenvalue of matrix m. Returns true if eigenvalue is an eigenvalue of m, false otherwise.
macro.example: 1) matrixIsEigVal($A, 2) returns true if 2 is an eigenvalue of A. 2) matrixIsEigVal($A, 0) tests if A is singular.
macro.gotcha: eigenvalue is a real scalar. This function tests only real eigenvalues. Returns a boolean. Internally checks if det(A - lambda*I) = 0.

macro.description: Tests whether the given array (not a matrix) is an eigenvector of matrix m. Returns true if it is an eigenvector, false otherwise.
macro.example: 1) matrixIsEigVec($A, array(1,0)) tests if [1,0] is an eigenvector of A. 2) matrixIsEigVec($A, matrixgetcol($A, 0, true)) tests the first column.
macro.gotcha: eigenvector must be a plain array, not a matrix object. A zero vector is never an eigenvector and will return false. Returns a boolean.

macro.description: Tests whether the row vectors of matrix m are linearly independent. Returns true if they are linearly independent, false if linearly dependent.
macro.example: 1) matrixIsRowsLinInd($A) returns true if no row is a linear combination of the others. 2) Use in answer checking: if (matrixIsRowsLinInd($stumatrix)) ...
macro.gotcha: Returns a boolean true or false. Internally uses row reduction, so floating-point precision can affect borderline cases.

macro.description: Returns the number of columns of matrix m as an integer.
macro.example: 1) matrixNumberOfColumns($A) returns 4 for a 3x4 matrix. 2) Used together with matrixNumberOfRows() to iterate over all entries.
macro.gotcha: Returns an integer scalar. Do not confuse with matrixNumberOfRows().

macro.description: Returns the number of rows of matrix m as an integer.
macro.example: 1) matrixNumberOfRows($A) returns 3 for a 3x2 matrix. 2) for ($i=0; $i<matrixNumberOfRows($A); $i++) iterates over rows.
macro.gotcha: Returns an integer scalar. Do not confuse with matrixNumberOfColumns(). Useful when the matrix dimensions are determined at runtime.

macro.description: Converts a student's matrix answer input into a single flat array of values. Use $stuanswers[$thisq] for single-part questions or getstuans($stuanswers, $thisq, partindex) for multi-part questions as the input.
macro.example: 1) $vals = matrixParseStuans($stuanswers[$thisq]); parses the student answer for a single-part matrix question. 2) $vals = matrixParseStuans(getstuans($stuanswers, $thisq, 1)); for a multi-part question.
macro.gotcha: Returns a flat array of values, not a matrix object. You will need to wrap the result in matrix() if you want a matrix object for comparison. The student's answer format depends on the question template used.

macro.description: Creates a matrix with random integer entries drawn uniformly from [minval, maxval], with dimensions rows x cols.
macro.example: 1) matrixRandomMatrix(-5, 5, 3, 3) creates a 3x3 matrix with entries between -5 and 5. 2) matrixRandomMatrix(0, 9, 2, 4) creates a 2x4 matrix with single-digit non-negative entries.
macro.gotcha: The resulting matrix may be singular. For problems where you need Ax=b to have a unique solution, use matrixrandinvertible() instead.

macro.description: Returns a matrix whose rows span the same row space as matrix m. The result may have the same number of rows as m or one additional row, giving a redundant (linearly dependent) spanning set for use in span problems.
macro.example: 1) $span = matrixRandomSpan($A); gives a spanning set for the row space of A. 2) Use with matrixAspansB() to check if a student's answer spans the correct space.
macro.gotcha: The returned matrix is not necessarily a basis — it may contain a linearly dependent row. Use matrixGetRowSpace() if you need a basis. The number of rows may differ from the input.

macro.description: Appends matrix n to the right side of matrix m, forming an augmented matrix. Both matrices must have the same number of rows.
macro.example: 1) matrixaugment($A, $b) creates [A|b] for solving Ax=b. 2) matrixaugment($A, matrixidentity(3)) creates [A|I] for computing inverses by row reduction.
macro.gotcha: Both matrices must have the same number of rows. The result has columns equal to cols(m) + cols(n). Use matrixdisplaytable with linemode=1 to display the augment line visually.

macro.description: Subtracts matrix n from matrix m element-wise and returns the resulting matrix. Both matrices must have the same dimensions.
macro.example: 1) matrixdiff($A, $B) returns A - B. 2) matrixformat(matrixdiff($A, $B)) formats the difference for display.
macro.gotcha: Order matters: matrixdiff($A, $B) computes A - B, not B - A. Both matrices must have identical dimensions.

macro.signature: matrixdisplaytable(m, [matrixname, displayASCIIticks, linemode, headernames, tablestyle, rownames, rowheader, caption])
macro.description: Generates an HTML table string for displaying a matrix, with options for augment lines, column/row headers, captions, and custom styles. Use linemode=1 for augmented matrices, linemode=2 for simplex tableau display.
macro.example: 1) matrixdisplaytable($A) renders a plain HTML table. 2) matrixdisplaytable($A, "A", 0, 1, array("x","y","b")) shows an augmented matrix with column headers. 3) matrixdisplaytable($A, "", 1) wraps each entry in ASCIIMath ticks.
macro.gotcha: All parameters after m are optional but positional — to supply a later parameter you must supply all earlier ones (or null). linemode=0 shows no lines, 1 shows augmented line, 2 shows simplex lines. displayASCIIticks=0 for answer-box matrices, 1 for rendered math display.

macro.description: Formats a matrix item into an ASCIIMath string suitable for display or for setting as $answer. Defaults to square brackets; pass '(' for parentheses or '\|' for absolute-value bars.
macro.example: 1) matrixformat($A) formats with square brackets. 2) matrixformat($A, "(") formats with round brackets. 3) $answer = matrixformat($A) sets the answer to the formatted matrix.
macro.gotcha: The bracket parameter must be a string: '[', '(', or '\|'. The output is a string, not a matrix object — do not pass it to other matrix functions that expect a matrix.

macro.description: Formats a matrix into an ASCIIMath string like matrixformat(), but converts decimal entries to fractions where possible. Use this after matrixinversefrac() or matrixsolvefrac() to display fraction results correctly.
macro.example: 1) matrixformatfrac($A) formats entries as fractions with square brackets. 2) matrixformatfrac($A, "(") uses round brackets. 3) $answer = matrixformatfrac(matrixinversefrac($A)) formats an inverse with fractions.
macro.gotcha: Entries that are already fraction strings (from matrixinversefrac or matrixsolvefrac) are handled correctly. Do not use this on matrices with entries that need to remain numeric for further calculations.

macro.description: Returns a specified column of matrix m as an n x 1 column matrix, or as a plain array if asArray is set to true. Column index is 0-indexed.
macro.example: 1) matrixgetcol($A, 0) returns the first column as an nx1 matrix. 2) matrixgetcol($A, 2, true) returns the third column as a plain array.
macro.gotcha: Column is 0-indexed. By default returns a column matrix object. Set asArray to true to get a plain array.

macro.description: Returns the scalar value of the entry at the given row and column of matrix m. Both row and col are 0-indexed.
macro.example: 1) matrixgetentry($A, 0, 0) returns the top-left entry. 2) matrixgetentry($A, 1, 2) returns the entry in the second row, third column.
macro.gotcha: Both row and col are 0-indexed. Requesting an out-of-bounds index will produce an error or unexpected result. Returns a scalar, not a matrix.

macro.description: Returns a specified row of matrix m as a 1 x n row matrix, or as a plain array if asArray is set to true. Row index is 0-indexed.
macro.example: 1) matrixgetrow($A, 0) returns the first row as a 1xn matrix. 2) matrixgetrow($A, 1, true) returns the second row as a plain array.
macro.gotcha: Row is 0-indexed. By default the return value is a 1 x n matrix object, not an array. Set asArray to true if you need a plain array for use with array functions.

macro.description: Extracts a submatrix from m using range selector strings in the format "start:end". Use ":" to select all rows or all columns.
macro.example: 1) matrixgetsubmatrix($A, "0:1", ":") selects the first two rows and all columns. 2) matrixgetsubmatrix($A, ":", "1:2") selects all rows and columns 2 and 3 (0-indexed). 3) matrixgetsubmatrix($A, "0:0", "0:1") selects a 1x2 submatrix from the top-left.
macro.gotcha: Selectors are strings in "start:end" format; indices are 0-indexed. The end index is inclusive. Use ":" alone to select all rows or columns.

macro.description: Creates and returns an n x n identity matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere.
macro.example: 1) matrixidentity(3) returns a 3x3 identity matrix. 2) matrixprod($A, matrixidentity(3)) verifies that A * I = A for a 3-column A.
macro.gotcha: n must be a positive integer. The result is a square matrix; there is no non-square version of this function.

macro.description: Computes and returns the inverse of an n x n square matrix m. Returns a matrix with decimal entries.
macro.example: 1) matrixinverse($A) returns A^-1. 2) matrixformat(matrixinverse($A)) formats the inverse for display. 3) matrixprod($A, matrixinverse($A)) should yield the identity (up to floating point).
macro.gotcha: The matrix must be square and invertible (non-singular). Entries are decimals; use matrixinversefrac() if you need fraction-formatted entries. Do not use the result in further matrix calculations if entries are non-integer.

macro.description: Computes the inverse of an n x n matrix m and returns it with entries expressed as fraction strings where possible. Use matrixformatfrac() to display the result.
macro.example: 1) $Ainv = matrixinversefrac($A); matrixformatfrac($Ainv) displays the inverse with fraction entries.
macro.gotcha: Entries are fraction strings, not numbers — do NOT use the result of this function in further matrix calculations such as matrixprod() or matrixsum(). It is for display only.

macro.description: Given an augmented matrix A already in reduced echelon form with n augment columns (right-hand sides), returns the count of equations Ax=b_i that have at least one solution.
macro.example: 1) matrixnumsolutions(matrixreduce($Ab, true), 1) returns 0 or 1 indicating consistency for a single b column. 2) matrixnumsolutions($rrefAB, 3) where $rrefAB has 3 augment columns returns how many systems are consistent.
macro.gotcha: A must already be in reduced echelon form (use matrixreduce() with rref=true first). n is the number of augment columns, not the total number of columns. Returns a count, not a boolean.

macro.description: Computes the matrix product m * n and returns the resulting matrix. The number of columns of m must equal the number of rows of n.
macro.example: 1) matrixprod($A, $B) returns AB. 2) matrixformat(matrixprod($A, $B)) formats the product. 3) matrixprod($A, matrixidentity(3)) returns A unchanged for a 3-column A.
macro.gotcha: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: matrixprod($A,$B) and matrixprod($B,$A) will generally differ. Inner dimensions must match or the result is undefined.

macro.description: Creates a random n x n invertible integer matrix by applying random row combinations to the identity matrix. Returns an array of two matrices: the matrix M and its inverse M^-1.
macro.example: 1) $pair = matrixrandinvertible(3); $M = $pair[0]; $Minv = $pair[1]; gives M and M^-1. 2) matrixformat($pair[0]) displays the random invertible matrix.
macro.gotcha: The return value is an array of two matrices, not a single matrix. Access the matrix with [0] and its inverse with [1]. Entries are integers, suitable for use in problems requiring exact arithmetic.

macro.description: Randomizes matrix m by applying n random row combinations, returning a new matrix in unreduced form. Sometimes includes additional operations to avoid a row of all zeros. Use this to create a "messy" version of a known matrix for row-reduction problems.
macro.example: 1) matrixrandunreduce($A, 3) applies 3 random row combinations to $A. 2) $rref = matrixreduce($A, true); $messy = matrixrandunreduce($rref, 4); generates a problem matrix from a known RREF.
macro.gotcha: In most cases this is preferred over matrixreduce() for generating problem matrices. The more row operations n, the more scrambled the result. Very large n can introduce large integer entries.

macro.description: Row-reduces matrix A to echelon form (default) or reduced row echelon form (RREF). Optionally returns entries as fraction strings. Note: in most authoring cases matrixrandunreduce() is a better choice than this function.
macro.example: 1) matrixreduce($A) reduces to echelon form with decimal entries. 2) matrixreduce($A, true) reduces to RREF. 3) matrixreduce($A, true, true) reduces to RREF with fraction entries.
macro.gotcha: When frac=true, entries are fraction strings — do not use the result in further calculations. The documentation notes that matrixrandunreduce() is usually preferable. rref defaults to false (echelon form).

macro.description: Rounds every entry of matrix m to the specified number of decimal places and returns the resulting matrix.
macro.example: 1) matrixround($A, 2) rounds all entries to 2 decimal places. 2) matrixround(matrixinverse($A), 4) rounds the inverse entries to 4 decimal places.
macro.gotcha: Rounding can introduce or hide floating-point artifacts. Use this for display purposes rather than for precision-critical computation.

macro.signature: matrixrowcombine(m, row1, a, row2, b, endrow)
macro.description: Replaces endrow in matrix m with the linear combination arow1 + brow2, and returns the resulting matrix. All row indices are 0-indexed. Used for elementary row operations during Gaussian elimination.
macro.example: 1) matrixrowcombine($A, 0, -2, 1, 1, 1) replaces row 1 with -2row0 + 1row1. 2) matrixrowcombine($A, 0, 1, 2, -3, 2) replaces row 2 with row0 - 3*row2.
macro.gotcha: All six arguments are required. endrow is the destination row index (0-indexed). Both row1 and row2 are read before writing, so endrow can equal row1 or row2 safely.

macro.signature: matrixrowcombine3(m, row1, a, row2, b, row3, c, endrow)
macro.description: Replaces endrow in matrix m with arow1 + brow2 + c*row3 and returns the resulting matrix. All row indices are 0-indexed. Extends matrixrowcombine() to three source rows.
macro.example: 1) matrixrowcombine3($A, 0, 1, 1, -2, 2, 1, 2) replaces row 2 with 1row0 - 2row1 + 1*row2.
macro.gotcha: All eight arguments are required. endrow can equal any of row1, row2, or row3 since source rows are read before the destination is written.

macro.description: Multiplies a single row of matrix m by the scalar n and returns the resulting matrix. Rows are 0-indexed.
macro.example: 1) matrixrowscale($A, 0, 2) multiplies the first row by 2. 2) matrixrowscale($A, 1, 1/3) scales the second row by 1/3.
macro.gotcha: Rows are 0-indexed: the first row is row 0, the second is row 1, and so on. The original matrix is not modified in-place; the function returns a new matrix.

macro.description: Swaps two rows in matrix m and returns the resulting matrix. Rows are 0-indexed.
macro.example: 1) matrixrowswap($A, 0, 1) swaps the first and second rows. 2) matrixrowswap($A, 1, 2) swaps rows 2 and 3 (0-indexed).
macro.gotcha: Rows are 0-indexed. Swapping a row with itself is a no-op but valid. The function returns a new matrix; the original is not changed.

macro.description: Multiplies every entry of matrix m by the scalar n and returns the resulting matrix.
macro.example: 1) matrixscalar($A, 3) multiplies all entries by 3. 2) matrixscalar($A, 1/2) scales by one-half. 3) matrixformat(matrixscalar($A, -1)) formats the negated matrix.
macro.gotcha: n is a scalar number, not a matrix. To multiply two matrices together use matrixprod() instead.

macro.description: Solves the matrix equation Ax = b where A is n x n and b is n x m, returning the n x m solution matrix x. Entries of x are decimals.
macro.example: 1) matrixsolve($A, $b) returns the solution matrix x such that Ax = b. 2) matrixformat(matrixsolve($A, $b)) formats the solution for display.
macro.gotcha: A must be square and invertible. b must be a matrix (not a plain array). If b is n x 1 the result is a column vector. For fraction entries use matrixsolvefrac().

macro.description: Solves Ax = b like matrixsolve() but returns the solution matrix with entries expressed as fraction strings. Use matrixformatfrac() to display the result.
macro.example: 1) $x = matrixsolvefrac($A, $b); matrixformatfrac($x) displays the fractional solution.
macro.gotcha: Entries may be fraction strings — do NOT use the result in further calculations. Use matrixsolve() if you need numeric entries for subsequent computation.

macro.description: Adds two matrices element-wise and returns the resulting matrix. Both matrices must have the same dimensions.
macro.example: 1) matrixsum($A, $B) returns the matrix A+B. 2) matrixformat(matrixsum($A, $B)) formats the sum for display.
macro.gotcha: Both matrices must be the same size; mismatched dimensions will produce incorrect results or errors. Returns a matrix object, not a scalar.

macro.description: Converts an augmented coefficient matrix into an ASCIIMath string displaying the equivalent system of linear equations. The last column is treated as the right-hand side constants.
macro.example: 1) matrixsystemdisp($A) uses default variables x, y, z. 2) matrixsystemdisp($A, array("a","b","c")) uses custom variable names. 3) matrixsystemdisp($A, null, false) hides the left bracket.
macro.gotcha: The matrix is expected to be an augmented matrix where the last column holds the constants. The variables array length should match the number of coefficient columns (total columns minus 1).

macro.description: Computes and returns the transpose of matrix m, swapping rows and columns so that entry (i,j) of the result equals entry (j,i) of the original.
macro.example: 1) matrixtranspose($A) returns A^T. 2) matrixformat(matrixtranspose($A)) formats the transpose for display. 3) matrixprod(matrixtranspose($A), $A) computes A^T * A.
macro.gotcha: For a non-square m x n matrix, the transpose is n x m. The original matrix is not modified.

macro.description: Finds the nth-degree polynomial that best fits the data arrays x and y using least-squares regression. Returns a flat array of coefficients in ascending order: [intercept, linear, quadratic, ...].
macro.example: 1) polyregression(array(1,2,3), array(2,5,10), 2) returns coefficients of the best-fit quadratic. 2) $c = polyregression($xdata, $ydata, 1); gives slope $c[1] and intercept $c[0].
macro.gotcha: The return value is a plain array of coefficients, not a matrix. The coefficient at index 0 is the constant term. x and y must be arrays of equal length with at least n+1 data points.

macro.description: Adds two polynomial objects and returns a new polynomial object. Like-degree terms are combined and the result is sorted by degree descending. Polynomials are represented as arrays of [coef, degree] term pairs.
macro.example: 1) addpolys(formpoly([1,2],2), formpoly([3,1],1)) adds x^2+2x and 3x+1 to get [[1,2],[5,1],[1,0]]. 2) addpolys(formpoly([1,0],2), formpoly([-1,0],2)) returns [[0,2]] (zero polynomial).
macro.gotcha: Terms with the same degree are combined but zero-coefficient terms are not automatically dropped. Pipe results through writepoly for display — the raw poly object is not a string.

macro.description: Checks whether the powers in a polynomial expression string appear in the requested order. Returns true if the order is correct, false otherwise. Useful for validating student-entered polynomial order.
macro.example: 1) checkpolypowerorder("3x^2 + 2x + 1") returns true (decreasing). 2) checkpolypowerorder("1 + 2x + 3x^2", "inc") returns true (increasing). 3) checkpolypowerorder("2x + 3x^2 + 1") returns false.
macro.gotcha: The function operates on an expression string, not a poly object. Terms without "^" are treated as degree 1 if non-numeric, else degree 0. Only "dec" and "inc" are valid ord values; default is "dec".

macro.description: Computes the derivative of a polynomial object using the power rule. Returns a new polynomial object. Constant terms (degree 0) are dropped.
macro.example: 1) derivepoly(formpoly([3,2,1],2)) differentiates 3x^2+2x+1 to return [[6,1],[2,0]]. 2) derivepoly(formpoly([5],0)) returns [] (derivative of a constant is zero).
macro.gotcha: The result is a poly object — use writepoly to get a display string. The constant term is dropped entirely; an all-constant polynomial returns an empty array, not [[0,0]].

macro.description: Generates a localized English text description of a polynomial function, suitable for screen-reader alt text. Evaluates the equation near roots and describes behavior at each x-intercept and at the ends.
macro.example: 1) describepoly("3(x-2)(x-3)", [2,3]) returns a sentence describing the polynomial's roots and end behavior. 2) describepoly("(x-1)^2", [1], "x", "f(x)", [[1,"local min"]]) adds a local minimum note at x=1.
macro.gotcha: xints must be an array — passing a non-array echoes a warning and returns "". Only describes roots with multiplicity 1 and 2. For rational functions with asymptotes, use describerational instead. Internally wraps describerational with empty asymptote lists.

macro.description: Generates a localized English text description of a rational function, including x-intercepts, vertical asymptotes, horizontal asymptote, and end behavior. Suitable for screen-reader alt text via replacealttext.
macro.example: 1) describerational("2(x-3)(x-2)/((x-4)*(x+1))", [2,3], [-1,4], 2) describes intercepts at x=2,3 and vertical asymptotes at x=-1,4 with horizontal asymptote y=2. 2) describerational("1/(x-2)", [], [2], null) describes only a vertical asymptote and infinite end behavior.
macro.gotcha: Both xints and vas must be arrays; invar and outvar must be strings — otherwise a warning is echoed and "" is returned. ha=null triggers end-behavior-as-infinity description. Returns "invalid function" if eqn cannot be parsed by makeMathFunction. Only handles multiplicity 1 and 2 behavior at roots and asymptotes.

macro.description: Performs polynomial long division of p1 by p2. Returns an array [quotient, remainder] where each element is a polynomial object. Both dividend and divisor must be polynomial objects.
macro.example: 1) divpolys(formpoly([1,0,-6],2), formpoly([1,-2],1)) divides x^2-6 by x-2 and returns [quotient poly, remainder poly]. 2) divpolys(formpoly([1,3],1), formpoly([2,1],1)) divides x+3 by 2x+1.
macro.gotcha: If the divisor is the zero polynomial (all coefficients near 0), returns [[], p1] — an empty quotient and the original dividend as remainder. Coefficients with absolute value less than 1e-12 are treated as zero. Access result[0] for quotient and result[1] for remainder.

macro.description: Creates a polynomial object from an array of coefficients and either an array of degrees or a single highest degree integer. When deg is an integer, degrees are assigned in descending order starting from deg. Use writepoly to display the result.
macro.example: 1) formpoly([3,2,1], 2) creates 3x^2 + 2x + 1. 2) formpoly([4,0,5], [3,1,0]) creates 4x^3 + 5. 3) formpoly("3,2,1", 2) also works with a comma-separated string.
macro.gotcha: If coef and deg arrays have different lengths, a warning is echoed and only overlapping indices are used. When deg is a scalar, degrees are assigned consecutively downward — a coef array of length 3 with deg=2 gives degrees [2,1,0]. Zero coefficients are kept in the object; writepoly will suppress them in the display by default.

macro.description: Builds a polynomial object as a * product of (x - root) factors. The leading scale factor a is applied to the entire product. Optionally supply a multiplicities array so roots are repeated the correct number of times.
macro.example: 1) formpolyfromroots(1, [2,3]) builds (x-2)(x-3) = x^2-5x+6. 2) formpolyfromroots(2, [1,-1]) builds 2(x-1)(x+1) = 2x^2-2. 3) formpolyfromroots(1, [0,1], [2,1]) builds x^2*(x-1) = x^3-x^2.
macro.gotcha: Complex root pairs are provided as a single [a,b] entry representing a+bi; the conjugate is handled automatically. If mult is omitted, all roots are assumed to have multiplicity 1. The stretch factor a is separate from the roots array — do not fold it into the roots list.

macro.description: Returns the coefficient of the x^deg term in polynomial object p. Returns 0 if no term with that degree exists in the polynomial.
macro.example: 1) getcoef(formpoly([3,2,1],2), 2) returns 3. 2) getcoef(formpoly([3,2,1],2), 0) returns 1. 3) getcoef(formpoly([3,2,1],2), 5) returns 0.
macro.gotcha: Returns 0 for any degree not explicitly present in the poly object, including degrees above the highest term. Do not use this to test whether a term exists — a coefficient of 0 in the object also returns 0.

macro.description: Multiplies two polynomial objects and returns a new polynomial object. All term pairs are multiplied, like-degree products are combined, and the result is sorted by degree descending.
macro.example: 1) multpolys(formpoly([1,1],1), formpoly([1,-1],1)) multiplies (x+1)(x-1) = x^2-1. 2) multpolys(formpoly([2,3],1), formpoly([1,0,1],2)) multiplies (2x+3)(x^2+1).
macro.gotcha: For repeated self-multiplication use polypower instead — it is more readable and equivalent. Results are a poly object; use writepoly for display. Very large polynomials multiplied together can produce many terms.

macro.description: Raises a polynomial object to a non-negative integer power using repeated multiplication. Returns a new polynomial object. pow must be an integer >= 1.
macro.example: 1) polypower(formpoly([1,1],1), 2) expands (x+1)^2 = x^2+2x+1. 2) polypower(formpoly([1,-1],1), 3) expands (x-1)^3 = x^3-3x^2+3x-1.
macro.gotcha: Performance degrades quickly for large pow values since repeated multiplication is used. pow=0 is not defined — use formpoly([1],0) for the constant 1 instead. For building a poly from roots, formpolyfromroots with a multiplicities array is cleaner than polypower on each factor.

macro.description: Returns the degree (highest power) of a polynomial object as an integer. Returns 0 for an empty polynomial object.
macro.example: 1) polys_getdegree(formpoly([3,2,1],2)) returns 2. 2) polys_getdegree(formpoly([5],0)) returns 0. 3) polys_getdegree([]) returns 0.
macro.gotcha: Returns 0 for both a degree-0 constant and an empty poly — these two cases are indistinguishable from this function alone. If you need to distinguish, check whether the poly array is empty separately.

macro.description: Solves the quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 using the quadratic formula. Returns [smallerRoot, largerRoot]. If the discriminant is negative (no real roots), returns ["DNE", "DNE"].
macro.example: 1) quadroot(1, -5, 6) returns [2, 3] (roots of x^2-5x+6). 2) quadroot(1, 0, -4) returns [-2, 2]. 3) quadroot(1, 0, 1) returns ["DNE","DNE"] (no real roots).
macro.gotcha: Does not handle a=0 — passing a=0 causes a division by zero. The roots are returned in sorted order [smaller, larger]. For checking whether roots exist, test if result[0] === "DNE" before using the numeric values.

macro.description: Rounds every coefficient in a polynomial object to d decimal places. Returns the updated polynomial object with rounded coefficients. Useful after floating-point arithmetic on poly objects.
macro.example: 1) roundpoly(formpoly([1.333, 2.666], 1), 2) returns a poly with coefficients [1.33, 2.67]. 2) roundpoly(derivepoly(formpoly([1,3,1],2)), 0) rounds derivative coefficients to integers.
macro.gotcha: Modifies and returns the polynomial in place. After rounding, near-zero coefficients become exactly 0 but are not removed from the term list — writepoly will suppress them in display by default. Choose d carefully; rounding too aggressively distorts the polynomial.

macro.description: Multiplies every coefficient in a polynomial object by the scalar constant c. Returns a new polynomial object with scaled coefficients.
macro.example: 1) scalepoly(formpoly([1,2,1],2), 3) scales x^2+2x+1 to 3x^2+6x+3. 2) scalepoly(formpoly([2,4],1), 0.5) scales 2x+4 to x+2. 3) scalepoly(formpoly([1,1],1), -1) negates all coefficients.
macro.gotcha: Passing c=0 produces a polynomial with all-zero coefficients — it is technically valid but writepoly will show nothing. If you want to negate a polynomial, use scalepoly(p, -1) rather than building a negated copy manually.

macro.description: Subtracts polynomial p2 from p1 (p1 - p2) and returns a new polynomial object. Like-degree terms are combined and the result is sorted by degree descending.
macro.example: 1) subtpolys(formpoly([3,2,1],2), formpoly([1,2,1],2)) subtracts to give 2x^2. 2) subtpolys(formpoly([1,0],1), formpoly([0,1],1)) computes x - 1 = [[1,1],[-1,0]].
macro.gotcha: Order matters — subtpolys(a,b) gives a-b, not b-a. Zero-coefficient terms from cancellation are retained in the poly object; writepoly suppresses them in the display by default.

macro.description: Converts a polynomial object to a display expression string such as "3 x^2 - 2 x + 1". The variable name, zero-term visibility, and fractional-coefficient formatting are all configurable.
macro.example: 1) writepoly(formpoly([3,2,1],2)) returns "3 x^2 + 2 x + 1". 2) writepoly(formpoly([1,0,1],2), "t") returns "t^2 + 1" (zero middle term suppressed). 3) writepoly(formpoly([1,0,1],2), "x", true) returns "x^2 + 0 x + 1" (zeros shown).
macro.gotcha: When sz=false (default) zero-coefficient terms are suppressed. Leading coefficient of 1 or -1 is shown as implicit (just the variable) for degree > 0 terms. For decimal coefficients that should display as fractions, use writepolyfrac or pass tofrac=true.

macro.description: Converts a polynomial object to a display string with decimal coefficients automatically converted to fractions where possible. Wrapper around writepoly with tofrac=true.
macro.example: 1) writepolyfrac(formpoly([0.5, 0.333], 1)) displays "1/2 x + 1/3" instead of "0.5 x + 0.333...". 2) writepolyfrac(scalepoly(formpoly([1,2,1],2), 0.25)) displays fractional coefficients cleanly.
macro.gotcha: Conversion uses decimaltofraction() — only decimal values that correspond to simple fractions will convert cleanly. Irrational or repeating decimals may not convert as expected. Use writepoly with tofrac=false when you want raw decimal display.

macro.description: Returns a random prime number drawn from precomputed tables. If digits is given (1–6), restricts results to primes with that many digits; passing 0 or omitting the argument returns a prime of mixed digit length.
macro.example: 1) getprime() — returns a random prime such as 17 or 1031. 2) getprime(2) — returns a random 2-digit prime such as 41. 3) getprime(1) — returns a single-digit prime: 2, 3, 5, or 7.
macro.gotcha: Only digit counts 1–6 are supported by the precomputed tables; values outside that range may return unexpected results. Randomness is driven by the IMathAS RNG seed, so results are reproducible per-seed. Use getprimes() when you need multiple distinct primes at once.

macro.description: Returns an array of n distinct random prime numbers. If digits is given (1–6), all returned primes have that digit length. Returns an empty array if digits is out of the supported range.
macro.example: 1) getprimes(3) — returns an array of 3 distinct primes, e.g., [7, 43, 307]. 2) getprimes(2, 2) — returns 2 distinct 2-digit primes, e.g., [13, 71].
macro.gotcha: Digit counts outside 1–6 cause an empty array to be returned silently. Requesting more primes than exist in a digit-length table (e.g., all 1-digit primes are 2, 3, 5, 7 — only 4) can produce unexpected behavior. Unlike getprime(), this function is deterministic relative to the RNG state only at the moment of the call.

macro.description: Returns true if n is a prime number, false otherwise. Uses trial division against precomputed small primes up to sqrt(n). Only works for positive integers less than 1,000,000.
macro.example: 1) isprime(17) — returns true. 2) isprime(18) — returns false. 3) isprime(999983) — returns true (largest prime below 1,000,000).
macro.gotcha: Inputs greater than 999999 or less than 1 trigger an echoed warning and return false — they are not silently coerced. Non-integer inputs also produce a warning. If you only need a prime to use in a problem, prefer getprime() rather than testing candidates with isprime().

macro.description: Reduces the quadratic radical expression (a + n*sqrt(rootnum)) / d to fully simplified form. Internally calls reduceradical on rootnum, then divides out the GCD across a, n, and d. Returns a string, display string, or parts array depending on format.
macro.example: 1) reducequadraticform(2, 4, 5, 2) — returns "(1+2sqrt(5))" after dividing GCD 2 from all parts. 2) reducequadraticform(1, 4, 5, 2, "parts") — returns array [1, 4, 5, 2]. 3) reducequadraticform(0, 3, -1, 1) — handles negative rootnum as complex, returning "3i".
macro.gotcha: When rootnum is negative and root is 2, the result includes i for imaginary unit. The a and n params are the rational and radical numerator coefficients respectively — do not confuse them with the HTML docs which label the params a, b, c, d. Pass format "disp" to get a backtick-wrapped string ready for IMathAS display.

macro.description: Reduces the radicand in under the given root degree, extracting perfect-power factors to produce A*root(B) in simplest form. Default root is 2 (square root). Returns a string, display string, parts array [outside, inside], or array depending on format.
macro.example: 1) reduceradical(50) — returns "5sqrt(2)" after extracting 25 from 50. 2) reduceradical(54, 3) — returns "3cbrt(2)" for cube root of 54. 3) reduceradical(50, 2, "parts") — returns array [5, 2].
macro.gotcha: The radicand is rounded to an integer internally — do not pass large floats. Even roots of negative numbers are treated as complex (includes i) for root=2, but produce an error for other even roots. Inputs greater than 1e10 may trigger a warning. root=0 or negative root values cause an error.

macro.description: Reduces the expression (n * root(rootnum)) / d by first simplifying the radical, then reducing the resulting fraction by GCD. Default root is 2. Returns a string, display string, or parts array [n, inside, d] depending on format.
macro.example: 1) reduceradicalfrac(4, 50, 2) — simplifies to (4*5sqrt(2))/2 then reduces to "10sqrt(2)". 2) reduceradicalfrac(3, 8, 6) — returns "sqrt(2)/2" after full reduction. 3) reduceradicalfrac(2, 9, 4, 2, "parts") — returns array with reduced parts.
macro.gotcha: Returns 0 in string modes when n=0 or rootnum=0. Radicands larger than 1e7 may trigger a warning and return null. Unsupported even roots of negative radicands produce an error. Non-finite inputs also cause an error and return 0. Use reduceradicalfrac2 when the radical is in the denominator instead.

macro.description: Reduces the expression num / (wholedenom * root(rootdenom)), simplifying the radical in the denominator and optionally rationalizing it. Default root is 2. Returns a string, display string, or parts array [n, d, inside] depending on format.
macro.example: 1) reduceradicalfrac2(2, 3, 5) — returns "2/(3sqrt(5))". 2) reduceradicalfrac2(2, 3, 5, true) — rationalizes denominator, returns "2sqrt(5)/15". 3) reduceradicalfrac2(4, 2, 4, false, 2, "parts") — returns reduced parts array.
macro.gotcha: The parameter order differs from reduceradicalfrac — the radical is in the denominator here, not the numerator. rationalize defaults to false; set true to clear the radical from the denominator. Internally implemented by transforming into a reduceradicalfrac call for some formats. Do not confuse with reduceradicalfrac3, which has radicals in both numerator and denominator.

macro.description: Reduces the expression (wholenum rootn(rootnum)) / (wholedenom rootd(rootdenom)), simplifying both radicals independently and reducing the resulting fraction. Default roots are both 2. Returns a string, display string, or parts array [wholenum, rootnum, wholedenom, rootdenom, root].
macro.example: 1) reduceradicalfrac3(2, 3, 5, 12) — simplifies both radicals and fraction; e.g., returns "(2sqrt(3))/(10sqrt(3))" reduced. 2) reduceradicalfrac3(1, 8, 1, 2, false, 3, 2) — uses cube root in numerator, square root in denominator. 3) reduceradicalfrac3(2, 50, 4, 8, false, 2, 2, "parts") — returns parts array [wholenum, rootnum, wholedenom, rootdenom, root].
macro.gotcha: rootn and rootd allow different root degrees for numerator and denominator — most other radical macros use a single root parameter. rationalize defaults to false. When radicals fully cancel between numerator and denominator the output collapses to a plain fraction string. For expressions with only one radical, use reduceradicalfrac or reduceradicalfrac2 instead.

macro.description: Returns n distinct random integers in [min, max]. One of the most commonly used array randomizers — ensures no repeated values among coefficients.
macro.example: 1) $a,$b = diffrands(-5, 5, 2) returns two different integers. 2) $a,$b,$c = diffrands(1, 10, 3, 'inc') returns three distinct integers in ascending order. 3) With where: $a,$b = diffrands(-5,5,2) where ($a+$b!=0).
macro.gotcha: The range [min, max] must contain at least n integers — too small a range causes an error. Can still return 0 — use nonzerodiffrands to exclude it.

macro.description: Returns n distinct elements from a list or array, without replacement. Use when picking several items from a fixed set and repeats are not allowed.
macro.example: 1) $a,$b = diffrandsfrom("10,20,30,40,50", 2) picks two different values. 2) $p,$q = diffrandsfrom($primes, 2, 'inc') picks two distinct primes in order.
macro.gotcha: The list must have at least n elements — fewer elements causes an error. Unlike randsfrom, no duplicates are possible.

macro.description: Returns n distinct random real numbers in [min, max] stepped by p. Real-valued version of diffrands.
macro.example: 1) $a,$b = diffrrands(0.5, 3.5, 0.5, 2) returns two distinct reals stepped by 0.5. 2) $x,$y = diffrrands(-2, 2, 0.1, 2, 'inc') returns two distinct reals in ascending order.
macro.gotcha: The number of grid points (max-min)/p + 1 must be >= n — too fine a range causes an error. Can return 0 — use nonzerodiffrrands to exclude it.

macro.description: Picks one random index, then returns the element at that index from each list. Use when list items are paired — e.g., names with prices, cities with populations — and you want a consistent pick across all lists.
macro.example: $item,$price = jointrandfrom("apple,banana,cherry", "1.20,0.50,2.00") — if index 1 is chosen: $item="banana", $price="0.50".
macro.gotcha: All lists must have the same number of elements — mismatched lengths produce undefined behavior. The number of assigned variables must equal the number of lists passed.

macro.description: Shuffles two lists simultaneously while keeping the pairing between corresponding elements intact. If n1 is given, returns the first n1 elements of each shuffled list (joint version of diffrandsfrom). If n2 is also given, returns n1 elements from list1 and n2 elements from list2.
macro.example: 1) $names,$scores = jointshuffle("Alice,Bob,Carol", "90,85,78") shuffles both while keeping pairs, e.g. ["Carol","Alice","Bob"] and ["78","90","85"]. 2) $a,$b = jointshuffle("1,2,3,4","a,b,c,d",2) returns first 2 pairs after shuffling.
macro.gotcha: Both lists must have equal length. When only n1 is given, both lists are trimmed to n1 elements. n2 allows different slice sizes per list — rarely needed.

macro.description: Returns n distinct nonzero integers in [min, max]. Combines diffrands and nonzerorand — use when all coefficients must be different and nonzero.
macro.example: $a,$b = nonzerodiffrands(-5, 5, 2) returns two distinct nonzero integers from -5 to 5.
macro.gotcha: The range must contain at least n nonzero integers. Example: nonzerodiffrands(-1, 1, 2) is valid (picks -1 and 1) but nonzerodiffrands(-1, 1, 3) will error.

macro.description: Returns n distinct nonzero real numbers in [min, max] stepped by p. Real-valued version of nonzerodiffrands.
macro.example: $a,$b = nonzerodiffrrands(-2, 2, 0.5, 2) returns two distinct nonzero reals stepped by 0.5.
macro.gotcha: Count of nonzero grid points must be >= n. Subtract 1 from total grid points if 0 lies on the grid.

macro.description: Returns a nonzero random integer in [min, max]. Use when zero would break the problem (denominator, leading coefficient, divisor).
macro.example: $a = nonzerorand(-5, 5) returns an integer from -5 to 5 excluding 0.
macro.gotcha: The range must contain at least one nonzero integer — nonzerorand(0, 0) will error. For arrays of nonzero integers use nonzerorands.

macro.description: Returns n nonzero random integers in [min, max]. Duplicates are allowed. Array version of nonzerorand.
macro.example: $a,$b = nonzerorands(-5, 5, 2) returns two nonzero integers from -5 to 5, possibly equal.
macro.gotcha: Duplicates allowed — use nonzerodiffrands if all values must be distinct. The range must contain at least one nonzero integer.

macro.description: Returns a nonzero random real number in [min, max] stepped by p. Combines rrand and nonzerorand.
macro.example: $a = nonzerorrand(-3, 3, 0.5) may return -2.5, -1.0, 1.5, etc. — never 0.
macro.gotcha: The grid (min..max step p) must contain at least one nonzero value. For multiple values use nonzerorrands.

macro.description: Returns n nonzero random real numbers in [min, max] stepped by p. Duplicates are allowed. Array version of nonzerorrand.
macro.example: $a,$b = nonzerorrands(-2, 2, 0.5, 2) returns two nonzero reals stepped by 0.5, possibly equal.
macro.gotcha: Duplicates allowed — use nonzerodiffrrands if all values must be distinct.

macro.description: Returns a random integer in [min, max] (inclusive). The most basic randomizer — use for simple integer coefficients or counters.
macro.example: 1) $a = rand(-5, 5) returns any integer from -5 to 5, including 0. 2) $n = rand(2, 10) returns an integer between 2 and 10.
macro.gotcha: Can return 0 — use nonzerorand if zero must be excluded. Returns only integers — use rrand for decimal steps. Does not return arrays — use rands for multiple values.

macro.description: Returns n random US or Canadian city names. country can be "USA" (default) or "Canada".
macro.example: 1) $c1,$c2 = randcities(2) returns two US cities. 2) $c1,$c2 = randcities(2,"Canada") returns two Canadian cities.
macro.gotcha: Duplicates possible. Defaults to USA — pass "Canada" explicitly for Canadian cities.

macro.description: Returns one random US or Canadian city name. country can be "USA" (default) or "Canada".
macro.example: 1) $city = randcity() may return "Chicago". 2) $city = randcity("Canada") may return "Toronto".
macro.gotcha: Returns the city name as a string. Defaults to USA — pass "Canada" explicitly for Canadian cities. For multiple cities use randcities.

macro.description: Returns n random country names from the world list. Use for multi-country comparison problems.
macro.example: $c1,$c2 = randcountries(2) may return "Brazil" and "Japan".
macro.gotcha: Duplicates possible. No region filter available.

macro.description: Returns one random country name from a world list. Use for context-independent geography problems.
macro.example: $country = randcountry() may return "Brazil" or "Japan".
macro.gotcha: No filter by region or continent — any country in the built-in list may be returned. For multiple countries use randcountries.

macro.description: Returns one random female first name. Use when the character is explicitly female and the problem text hard-codes she/her/hers.
macro.example: $name = randfemalename() may return "Maria" or "Emily".
macro.gotcha: Returns the name only — pronouns must be hard-coded. For arrays of female names use randfemalenames.

macro.description: Returns n random female first names. Use for multi-character problems where all characters are explicitly female.
macro.example: $n1,$n2 = randfemalenames(2) may return "Maria" and "Emily".
macro.gotcha: Duplicates possible. No pronouns — hard-code she/her/hers in the problem text.

macro.description: Returns one random element from a list or array. A list is a quoted comma-separated string. Use for picking from a fixed discrete set (numbers, strings, or expressions).
macro.example: 1) $a = randfrom("2,4,6,8") picks one even number. 2) $color = randfrom("red,green,blue") picks a color. 3) $n = randfrom($myarray) picks from a pre-built array.
macro.gotcha: When the list contains numbers as strings, the result is a string type — be careful with arithmetic. Different from diffrandsfrom: multiple independent randfrom calls can pick the same element.

macro.description: Returns one random male first name. Use when the character is explicitly male and the problem text hard-codes he/him/his.
macro.example: $name = randmalename() may return "James" or "Michael".
macro.gotcha: Returns the name only — pronouns must be hard-coded in the question text. For arrays of male names use randmalenames.

macro.description: Returns n random male first names. Use for multi-character problems where all characters are explicitly male.
macro.example: $n1,$n2 = randmalenames(2) may return "James" and "Robert".
macro.gotcha: Duplicates possible. No pronouns — hard-code he/him/his in the problem text.

macro.description: Returns one random first name (gender-neutral pool). Use in word problems that need a character name without specifying gender.
macro.example: $name = randname() may return "Alex" or "Jordan".
macro.gotcha: Returns the name only — no pronouns. Use randnamewpronouns if pronouns (he/she/they) are needed in the problem text.

macro.description: Returns n random first names from the gender-neutral pool. Use for multi-character word problems that do not specify gender.
macro.example: $n1,$n2 = randnames(2) may return "Alex" and "Jordan".
macro.gotcha: Duplicates are possible — two characters may get the same name. No pronouns included.

macro.description: Returns a random first name plus five pronouns in order: subjective (he/she/they), objective (him/her/them), possessive-singular (his/her/their), possessive-plural (his/hers/theirs), reflexive (himself/herself/themself). Pass 'neutral' to force they/them regardless of name gender.
macro.example: $name,$heshe,$himher,$hisher,$hishers,$himherself = randnamewpronouns() may yield: "Maria","she","her","her","hers","herself". Use $heshe in text: "$name went to the store. $heshe bought milk."
macro.gotcha: Must assign all 6 variables in order — missing variables will be lost. This is the only Randomizers macro that returns 6 values. Pass 'neutral' explicitly if gender-neutral pronouns are always required.

macro.description: Returns a Pythagorean triple (a, b, c) satisfying a^2 + b^2 = c^2. min/max constrain the leg values (default 1 to 100). Use for right-triangle problems requiring clean integer sides.
macro.example: 1) $a,$b,$c = randpythag() may return 3,4,5 or 5,12,13. 2) $a,$b,$c = randpythag(1,20) returns a triple with legs <= 20.
macro.gotcha: Always assign exactly 3 variables. c is always the hypotenuse (largest value). min/max apply to the legs, not the hypotenuse — the hypotenuse may exceed max.

macro.description: Returns n random integers in [min, max]. Duplicates are allowed. order can be 'inc' or 'dec' to sort, but duplicates may still appear. Use when you need several independent integer random values.
macro.example: 1) $a,$b,$c = rands(1, 10, 3) returns three integers 1–10, possibly with repeats. 2) $vals = rands(1, 5, 5, 'inc') returns 5 sorted integers, possibly with repeats.
macro.gotcha: Duplicates are allowed — use diffrands if all values must be distinct. Sorting with 'inc'/'dec' does not remove duplicates.

macro.description: Returns n elements picked randomly from a list or array, with replacement (duplicates allowed). Array version of randfrom.
macro.example: 1) $a,$b = randsfrom("1,2,3,4,5", 2) picks two elements, possibly the same. 2) $vals = randsfrom($options, 3, 'inc') picks 3 elements sorted ascending.
macro.gotcha: With replacement — same element can appear multiple times. Use diffrandsfrom if all picks must be distinct. Number strings from a quoted list remain strings.

macro.description: Returns one random US state or Canadian province name. country can be "USA" (default) or "Canada".
macro.example: 1) $state = randstate() may return "Texas". 2) $prov = randstate("Canada") may return "Ontario".
macro.gotcha: Returns the full name, not the abbreviation (e.g., "California" not "CA"). Defaults to USA. For multiple states use randstates.

macro.description: Returns n random US state or Canadian province names. country can be "USA" (default) or "Canada".
macro.example: 1) $s1,$s2 = randstates(2) returns two US state names. 2) $p1,$p2 = randstates(2,"Canada") returns two Canadian province names.
macro.gotcha: Returns full names, not abbreviations (e.g., "California" not "CA"). Duplicates possible.

macro.description: Returns a random real number in [min, max] stepped by p. Use for decimals with a fixed precision: prices, probabilities, or decimal coefficients.
macro.example: 1) $x = rrand(2, 5, 0.1) may return 3.4. 2) $r = rrand(2, 8, 2) returns 2, 4, 6, or 8. 3) $p = rrand(0.1, 0.9, 0.01) returns a 2-decimal probability.
macro.gotcha: The step p must divide the range evenly. Can return 0 if 0 lies on the grid — use nonzerorrand to exclude it. Not for arrays — use rrands for multiple values.

macro.description: Returns n random real numbers in [min, max] stepped by p. Duplicates are allowed. Array version of rrand.
macro.example: 1) $a,$b = rrands(1, 5, 0.5, 2) returns two reals stepped by 0.5, possibly equal. 2) $vals = rrands(0, 1, 0.1, 4, 'inc') returns 4 sorted probabilities.
macro.gotcha: Duplicates allowed — use diffrrands if all values must be distinct. Step p must divide the range evenly.

macro.description: Returns a shuffled version of a list or array. If n is given, returns the first n elements of the shuffled list — equivalent to diffrandsfrom.
macro.example: 1) $arr = singleshuffle("1,2,3,4,5") may return ["3","1","5","2","4"]. 2) $a,$b,$c = singleshuffle($options, 3) returns 3 distinct random elements from $options.
macro.gotcha: Without n, the full list is returned shuffled. Result is always an array — access with index [0],[1],... or multi-variable assignment.

macro.description: Finds the 0 (min), 1st, 2nd (median), 3rd, or 4th (max) quartile of a data array using the Excel inclusive method, matching Excel's QUARTILE and QUARTILE.INC functions. Uses linear interpolation.
macro.example: 1) Excelquartile($a, 1) returns Q1 matching Excel QUARTILE.INC. 2) Excelquartile($a, 3) returns Q3.
macro.gotcha: This matches the inclusive Excel method (QUARTILE.INC). For the exclusive Excel method use Excelquartileexc. Results differ from TI-84 and Triola methods on small or odd-sized datasets.

macro.description: Finds the 0 (min), 1st, 2nd (median), 3rd, or 4th (max) quartile of a data array using the Excel QUARTILE.EXC method, which excludes the 0th and 4th quartile boundary cases.
macro.example: 1) Excelquartileexc($a, 1) returns Q1 matching Excel QUARTILE.EXC. 2) Excelquartileexc($a, 3) returns Q3.
macro.gotcha: QUARTILE.EXC cannot compute Q0 or Q4 and will fail for very small datasets. Use Excelquartile for the inclusive version.

macro.description: Finds the given percentile of a data array using the p/100*(N+1) locator method, as recommended by OpenStax. Returns a numeric value from or interpolated between the dataset.
macro.example: 1) Nplus1percentile($a, 30) finds the 30th percentile using OpenStax method. 2) Nplus1percentile([1,2,3,4,5], 50) returns the median.
macro.gotcha: Results differ from percentile() because the locator formula uses N+1 instead of N. Use this when the course follows OpenStax or N+1 conventions.

macro.description: Finds the 0 (min), 1st, 2nd (median), 3rd, or 4th (max) quartile using the N+1 percentile method, as used by OpenStax. Returns a numeric value.
macro.example: 1) Nplus1quartile($a, 1) returns Q1 using OpenStax N+1 method. 2) Nplus1quartile($a, 2) returns the median.
macro.gotcha: Uses the p/100*(N+1) locator, which can interpolate between data values. Match this to courses that use Nplus1percentile for consistency.

macro.description: Finds the 0 (min), 1st, 2nd (median), 3rd, or 4th (max) quartile of a data array using the TI-84 calculator method, which splits the dataset at the median and finds the median of each half.
macro.example: 1) TIquartile($a, 1) returns Q1 as computed by a TI-84. 2) TIquartile($a, 3) returns Q3.
macro.gotcha: The TI-84 method excludes the median from both halves when N is odd before computing Q1 and Q3. Results will differ from Excel and Triola methods, especially for small datasets.

macro.description: Computes the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of an array of numbers: the average of the absolute differences between each data value and the mean. Returns a non-negative number.
macro.example: 1) absmeandev([2,4,6,8]) returns 2. 2) absmeandev([1,1,1,1]) returns 0.
macro.gotcha: Not the same as standard deviation. No optional weights parameter. Array must be non-empty.

macro.description: Computes the specified quartile using all available quartile methods and returns an "or"-joined string of all unique answers. Useful for accepting multiple correct answers in a question.
macro.example: 1) allquartile($a, 1) might return "5 or 5.5 or 6" if methods disagree on Q1. 2) allquartile($a, 2) returns the median (all methods agree).
macro.gotcha: The returned value is a string, not a number. It is intended to be used as the $answer variable directly so IMathAS accepts any of the listed values. Do not use for numeric computation.

macro.description: Performs one-way ANOVA on two or more groups and returns the full ANOVA table as a nested array: [[SS_A, df_A, MS_A, F_A, P_A], [SS_E, df_E, MS_E], [SS_T, df_T]]. Accepts unequal sample sizes.
macro.example: 1) $tbl = anova1way($g1,$g2,$g3); $F=$tbl[0][3]; $p=$tbl[0][4]; extracts F and p. 2) anova_table(anova1way($g1,$g2,$g3)) displays the ANOVA table.
macro.gotcha: Returns a nested array, not a display string. Pass the result to anova_table() for a formatted HTML table. Rows: index 0=Factor A, 1=Error, 2=Total. Column order: SS, df, MS, F, P (error and total rows have fewer columns).

macro.description: Performs one-way ANOVA on two or more groups and returns the F ratio and corresponding p-value as an array [F, P]. Accepts unequal sample sizes. Use this for quick F/p extraction without the full ANOVA table.
macro.example: 1) $res = anova1way_f($g1, $g2, $g3); $F=$res[0]; $p=$res[1]; gets F ratio and p-value for 3 groups.
macro.gotcha: Requires at least 2 group arrays. All group arrays must contain numeric data. For the full ANOVA table use anova1way() followed by anova_table(). The p-value is the right-tail probability from the F-distribution.

macro.description: Performs two-way ANOVA with or without replication and returns a nested ANOVA table array. With replication=false (default) returns rows for Factor A, Factor B, Error, Total. With replication=true also returns an Interaction row.
macro.example: 1) $tbl = anova2way($arr) runs two-way ANOVA without replication. 2) $tbl = anova2way($arr, true) includes the A*B interaction row.
macro.gotcha: The input arr format differs between with/without replication: without replication arr is a 2D array (one value per cell); with replication each cell is an array of replicates. Pass result to anova_table() with matching factor=2 and replication settings.

macro.description: Performs two-way ANOVA and returns only the F ratios and p-values as a nested array: [[F_A, P_A], [F_B, P_B], [F_I, P_I]] (interaction row only present when replication=true).
macro.example: 1) $res = anova2way_f($arr); $FA=$res[0][0]; $pA=$res[0][1]; gets F and p for Factor A. 2) $res = anova2way_f($arr, true); $FI=$res[2][0]; gets interaction F ratio.
macro.gotcha: The arr format is the same as anova2way(). The interaction row [F_I, P_I] is only included when replication=true. For the full ANOVA table use anova2way() with anova_table().

macro.description: Display macro. Converts the output of anova1way() or anova2way() into a formatted HTML ANOVA table for display. factor=1 for one-way (default), factor=2 for two-way. replication matches the anova2way call. nameA and nameB customize factor labels.
macro.example: 1) anova_table(anova1way($g1,$g2,$g3)) displays a one-way ANOVA table. 2) anova_table(anova2way($arr,true), 2, true, 12, "Treatment","Block") displays a two-way ANOVA table with replication.
macro.gotcha: The arr input must come from anova1way() or anova2way() — do not build the array manually. The roundto parameter (default 12) controls displayed precision. factor must match the anova function used.

macro.description: Computes the left-tail cumulative probability under the beta distribution with parameters alpha and beta. Returns P(X <= x) for x in [0,1]. The beta distribution models proportions and probabilities.
macro.example: 1) beta_cdf(0.5, 2, 3) returns P(X <= 0.5) for Beta(2,3). 2) beta_cdf(0.3, 1, 1) returns 0.3 (uniform distribution).
macro.gotcha: x must be between 0 and 1. Both alpha and beta must be positive. Despite the description in the source referencing gamma, this correctly computes the beta CDF.

macro.description: Inverse beta CDF. Returns the x value in [0,1] such that the left-tail probability under the beta distribution with parameters alpha and beta equals p.
macro.example: 1) beta_inv(0.5, 2, 3) returns the median of Beta(2,3). 2) beta_inv(0.95, 5, 2) returns the 95th percentile.
macro.gotcha: p must be strictly between 0 and 1. alpha and beta must both be positive. Uses numerical inversion; extreme p values near 0 or 1 may have reduced precision.

macro.description: Computes the cumulative binomial probability P(X <= x): the probability of at most x successes in N trials with success probability p. Returns a value between 0 and 1.
macro.example: 1) binomialcdf(10, 0.3, 4) returns P(X<=4). 2) binomialcdf(20, 0.5, 10) returns P(X<=10) for a fair coin.
macro.gotcha: This is a left-tail (cumulative) CDF. For P(X >= k) compute 1 - binomialcdf(N, p, k-1). For P(X = k) use binomialpdf. x must be a non-negative integer <= N.

macro.description: Computes the binomial probability P(X = x): the probability of exactly x successes in N independent trials each with success probability p. Returns a value between 0 and 1.
macro.example: 1) binomialpdf(10, 0.3, 4) returns P(X=4) for B(10,0.3). 2) binomialpdf(20, 0.5, 10) returns P(X=10) for a fair coin flipped 20 times.
macro.gotcha: x must be a non-negative integer and x <= N. p must be between 0 and 1 inclusive. For cumulative probability use binomialcdf.

macro.description: Display macro. Draws an SVG box-and-whisker plot for a data array. Supports comparative boxplots when array is an array of arrays. Options control quartile method, outlier display, value labels, and width.
macro.example: 1) boxplot($data, "Heights") draws a single boxplot. 2) boxplot([$d1,$d2], "Score", ['datalabels'=>['Group A','Group B'], 'showvals'=>true]) draws comparative boxplots with 5-number summaries.
macro.gotcha: Options array keys: datalabels (array), showvals (true/false), showoutliers (true/false), qmethod ('N','TI','Excel','Nplus1'), width. Default qmethod is 'N'. For backwards compatibility, the 3rd argument can be a plain array of datalabels.

macro.signature: checkdrawnlineagainstdata(xarray, yarray, studentanswer, [gradedots, alpha, grid, snaptogrid])
macro.description: Grading helper for drawn-line questions. Checks whether a student's drawn line (from a draw-type question) falls within confidence bounds of the regression line. Returns array(answer, showanswer).
macro.example: 1) list($answer,$showanswer) = checkdrawnlineagainstdata($x,$y,$stuanswers[$thisq]); grades a drawn line.
macro.gotcha: studentanswer must be the raw $stuanswers[$thisq] from a draw input type. gradedots=true will additionally check that the scatter plot dots were plotted. Pass grid and snaptogrid if those options were set on the graph.

macro.description: Grading helper. Checks whether a student's line equation (e.g., "2x+3") falls within confidence bounds of the regression line for the given data. Returns array(answer, showanswer) to assign to $answer and $showanswer.
macro.example: 1) list($answer,$showanswer) = checklineagainstdata($x,$y,$stuanswers[$thisq]); grades a student's typed line equation.
macro.gotcha: The student answer must be a line equation string using the variable (default "x"). alpha defaults to 0.05 for confidence bounds. This handles the grading logic; do not compare the student answer to a fixed regression equation manually.

macro.description: Computes the left-tail cumulative probability under the chi-squared distribution with df degrees of freedom up to x. Returns P(chi2 <= x). Use for chi-squared hypothesis tests.
macro.example: 1) chi2cdf(5.991, 2) returns approximately 0.95. 2) chi2cdf(9.488, 4) returns approximately 0.95.
macro.gotcha: x must be non-negative. df must be a positive integer. This is a left-tail CDF; for a right-tail p-value (as used in chi-squared tests) compute 1 - chi2cdf(teststat, df).

macro.description: Computes the chi-squared test statistic sum((O-E)^2/E) given a matrix of expected and observed values. The matrix m contains (O-E)^2/E terms, or equivalently the function computes the sum across all cells.
macro.example: 1) $chi2 = chi2teststat($matrix) where $matrix contains the chi-squared contribution of each cell.
macro.gotcha: The input matrix m should contain the pre-computed cell contributions (O-E)^2/E, one per cell. The function sums them. To get the p-value, follow with 1-chi2cdf($chi2, df) or fcdf equivalent.

macro.description: Computes the chi-squared CDF: the left-tail area under the chi-squared distribution with a degrees of freedom up to x. Returns a probability. This is an internal/lower-level function; prefer chi2cdf for general use.
macro.example: 1) chicdf(5.991, 2) returns approximately 0.95.
macro.gotcha: This is a lower-level implementation. For most question-writing use chi2cdf instead. The parameter order is (x, degrees_of_freedom). x must be non-negative.

macro.signature: cluster_bargraph(var1labels, var2labels, freqarray, label, [width, height, options])
macro.description: Display macro. Creates a clustered (grouped) bar chart for two categorical variables. var1labels are the horizontal axis categories (clusters); var2labels appear in the legend. freqarray is an array of arrays, one per var2 category, each containing one height per var1 category.
macro.example: 1) cluster_bargraph(['Low','Med','High'],['Male','Female'],[[10,15,8],[12,9,11]],"Frequency") creates a 3-cluster, 2-series bar chart.
macro.gotcha: freqarray structure: freqarray[j] contains the bar heights for var2 category j across all var1 categories. So freqarray should have length equal to the number of var2 categories, and each inner array should have length equal to the number of var1 categories. Options support: colors (array), stroke, gap, toplabel, vertlabel, var1name, var2name.

macro.description: Returns the count of items in an array that satisfy a string condition. The condition uses x as the placeholder for each data value. Useful for computing frequencies without creating classes.
macro.example: 1) countif($a, "x<3 && x>2") counts values strictly between 2 and 3. 2) countif($a, "x>=60 && x<70") counts values in the 60s. 3) countif($a, "x==5") counts values equal to 5.
macro.gotcha: The condition is a string with x as the variable name. Use == for equality (not =). Logical operators && and || are supported. The comparison is evaluated as PHP, so floating-point precision issues may arise near boundaries.

macro.description: Display macro. Creates a hyperlink that, when clicked, downloads the specified data columns as a CSV file. Each column is specified by a header string followed by an array of values. An optional filename (without .csv) may be provided as the first argument.
macro.example: 1) csvdownloadlink("data","Height",$heights,"Weight",$weights) creates a download link for a two-column CSV. 2) csvdownloadlink("Height",$h) creates a single-column CSV with no custom filename.
macro.gotcha: The filename argument is optional; if omitted the first argument should be the header string. Column arrays must all be the same length. The download is triggered client-side; no server file is created.

macro.description: Display macro. Creates an SVG dot plot from a raw data array. Data values are rounded to the nearest dotspacing increment and stacked as dots. The label appears below the horizontal axis.
macro.example: 1) dotplot($data, "Test Scores") creates a basic dot plot. 2) dotplot($data, "Ages", 1, 5, 400, 200) sets dot spacing=1, axis label every 5, and 400x200 px size.
macro.gotcha: Data is rounded to the nearest dotspacing value (default 1). Choose dotspacing to match data granularity, otherwise values will be grouped incorrectly. Default size is 300x150 px. labelspacing defaults to dotspacing if not set.

macro.description: Returns an array of n random numbers drawn from an exponential distribution with mean mu. Optional rnd specifies decimal rounding (default 3). Use for modeling waiting times or decay processes.
macro.example: 1) expdistrand(5, 20) generates 20 exponentially distributed values with mean 5. 2) expdistrand(10, 30, 1) generates 30 values rounded to 1 decimal.
macro.gotcha: The parameter mu is the mean, not the rate. The rate lambda = 1/mu. All values will be positive. Results are random each evaluation unless seeded.

macro.description: Computes the exponential regression fit for paired x and y data. Returns an array [r, base, intercept] where r is the correlation coefficient, and the model is intercept * base^x.
macro.example: 1) $res = expreg($x, $y); $r=$res[0]; $b=$res[1]; $a=$res[2]; gives r, base, intercept.
macro.gotcha: The y data must be all positive (logarithm is taken internally). The returned model is y = intercept * base^x, not the linearized form.

macro.description: Returns the right-tail probability (area to the right of f) under the F-distribution with df1 numerator and df2 denominator degrees of freedom. This is technically 1 minus the CDF. Use for ANOVA and regression F-tests.
macro.example: 1) fcdf(4.26, 1, 20) returns the right-tail p-value for F=4.26 with df1=1, df2=20. 2) fcdf(3.49, 3, 20) returns the p-value for an ANOVA F-ratio.
macro.gotcha: This function returns the right-tail area (p-value), not the left-tail CDF, unlike most CDF functions in the library. Algorithm is accurate to approximately 4-5 decimal places. f must be non-negative.

macro.description: Display macro. Creates a bar graph where bars are explicitly labeled (not class-interval based). Takes an array of bar labels and a matching array of frequencies or heights. Used for categorical data displays.
macro.example: 1) fdbargraph(['A','B','C','D'], [10,15,8,12], "Grade") creates a labeled bar chart. 2) fdbargraph($labels, $counts, "Color", 400, 300, ['gap'=>0.2, 'fill'=>'red']) adds gap and color.
macro.gotcha: Bar labels and frequency arrays must be the same length. Options array supports: valuelabels, showgrid, vertlabel, gap (0 to <1), toplabel, fill, stroke. This is for categorical bar graphs, not histograms.

macro.signature: fdhistogram(freqarray, label, start, classwidth, [labelstart, upper, width, height, showgrid, fill, stroke])
macro.description: Display macro. Creates an SVG histogram from a pre-computed frequency array (such as the output of frequency()). Parameters mirror histogram() but the first argument is an array of frequencies, not raw data.
macro.example: 1) $f = frequency($data, 60, 5, 90); fdhistogram($f, "Height", 60, 5) creates histogram from freq array. 2) fdhistogram($f, "Score", 0, 10, 0, 10, ['valuelabels'=>true]) adds frequency labels above bars.
macro.gotcha: The 5th argument can be an associative array of options, allowing 'vertlabel' and 'valuelabels'=>true. If raw data is available, histogram() is simpler; use fdhistogram when you need the frequency array separately.

macro.description: Returns the unique mode of the data array. If the data does not have exactly one mode, the function modifies the data array in-place to ensure a single unique mode exists before returning it.
macro.example: 1) $mode = forceonemode($data); guarantees $data has one mode and returns it.
macro.gotcha: This function can alter the passed array as a side effect. Always call forceonemode before any other functions that use the same data array, or the data may be unexpectedly modified. Do not use if data integrity must be preserved.

macro.description: Display macro. Returns an HTML frequency distribution table grouping the data into classes. The table shows lower class limits, upper class limits, and frequencies.
macro.example: 1) freqdist($data, "Height", 60, 5) produces a frequency table with class width 5 starting at 60.
macro.gotcha: This is a display-only macro; it returns HTML, not an array. Use frequency() if you need the numeric frequency array for further computation. The first lower class limit is start; the first upper limit is start+classwidth-1 (for integers).

macro.description: Returns a numeric array of frequencies for data grouped into classes. Each element is the count of data values in that class. Providing the optional end value ensures the last class is always included.
macro.example: 1) frequency($data, 60, 5) returns an array of counts per class. 2) frequency($data, 60, 5, 90) ensures a class up to 90 is included.
macro.gotcha: Without the end parameter the last class may be omitted if no data falls there. The end parameter is highly recommended to ensure the array matches your intended number of classes.

macro.description: Computes the left-tail cumulative probability under the gamma distribution with the given shape parameter. Optional scale (default 1) and offset shift the distribution. Returns P(X <= x).
macro.example: 1) gamma_cdf(3, 2) returns the gamma CDF at x=3 with shape=2 and default scale=1. 2) gamma_cdf(5, 3, 2) uses scale=2.
macro.gotcha: x must be greater than offset (or >= 0 by default). shape and scale must be positive. The gamma distribution includes exponential (shape=1) and chi-squared (shape=df/2, scale=2) as special cases.

macro.description: Inverse gamma CDF. Returns the x value such that the left-tail probability under the gamma distribution with the given shape and optional scale equals p.
macro.example: 1) gamma_inv(0.95, 2) returns the 95th percentile of a gamma(2,1) distribution. 2) gamma_inv(0.5, 3, 2) returns the median with shape=3, scale=2.
